 - **120-2**  There is no general rule as to whether or not the **kitchen** is included in the number of rooms.
 - **120-5**  **Overcrowded**, adj. - **overcrowding**, n.
ctx_en.en:14:
The occupier of a dwelling may be its **owner** **(121-1)** or a **tenant** **(121-2)** who rents it from an owner, who is then called **landlord** **(121-1)**. A tenant who rents a dwelling to a sub-tenant is called the **principal tenant** **(121-5)**. A **sub-tenant** **(121-3)** is a person who rents from a tenant. A person occupying a dwelling to which he or she has no legal title is called a **squatter** **(121-4)** .
 - **121-2** A dwelling or apartment may be rented with or without furniture in which case it is respectively called a **furnished dwelling** or an **unfurnished dwelling**.
ctx_en.en:15:
The terms **population statistics** **(130-1)** or **demographic statistics** **(130-1)** refer to **numerical data** **(130-2)** about populations, which are based on **observations** **(130-3)** . After such observations have been **collected** **(130-4)** on appropriate *forms* (206-1), the documents are **edited** **(130-5)** and **verified** **(130-5)** to eliminate obvious inconsistencies. The data are **tabulated** **(130-6)** into certain **groups** **(130-7)** or **classes** **(130-8)** with common characteristics. **Data processing** **(130-9)** includes all the steps between collecting and **statistical analysis** **(130-10)** (132-1).
 - **130-1**  **Statistics**, n. - **statistical**, adj. - **statistician**, n.: specialist in statistics.
 - **130-4**  **Collect**, v. - **collection**, n.
 - **130-5**  **Edit**, v. - **editing**, n. **Verify**, v. - **verification**, n.
 - **130-6**  **Tabulate**, v. - **tabulation**, n.
 - **130-9**  **Process**, v. - **processing**, n.
ctx_en.en:16:
Data are usually referred to as **raw data** **(131-1)** or **crude data** **(131-1)** prior to their *processing* and *tabulation* and **basic data** **(131-1)** or **primary data** **(131-1)** after processing and tabulation. Basic data usually consist of **series** **(131-2)** of **absolute numbers** **(131-3)** which are put together in the form of **statistical tables** **(131-4)** . In such tables the data are generally classified with respect to certain **variables** **(131-5)** or **variates** **(131-5)** such as age, number of children, etc., or with respect to certain **attributes** **(131-6)** or **characteristics** **(131-6)** (i.e. sex, marital status, etc.). Where data are classified with respect to several variables or attributes simultaneously the tables are called **cross-tabulations** **(131-7)** or **contingency tables** **(131-7)** . **Summary tables** **(131-8)** give information in less detail than do **individual tables** **(131-9)** .
 - **131-1**  When the data relate to *individuals* (110-2) as their unit of analysis they may be referred to as micro-data. Aggregate data or macro-data relate to a unit of analysis other than an individual, for example, a nation or an administrative unit within a nation. Micro-data can be derived from several sources such as a *field survey* (203-5) or a sample of vital registration records. A new source of micro-data is the census public use sample, which is a systematic or a random sample of census returns that is made available for analytical purposes to interested individuals.
 - **131-7**  A table which presents the distribution of a single variable or attribute within a population is generally called a **frequency table**.
ctx_en.en:17:
Using the basic data generally involves two phases. **Analysis** **(132-1)** aims at isolating the components of the observed numbers (size, structure, extraneous factors and the phenomenon under investigation); **synthesis** **(132-2)** is the process of recombining the disaggregated components in various ways. Either phase involves the **calculation** **(132-3)** or **computation** **(132-3)** of **indices** **(132-4)** which may be denoted by various names (cf. § 133). In contrast to the basic data, these indices are referred to as **results** **(132-6)** or **synthetic indices** **(132-5)**. In a more restricted sense an **index** **(132-7)** (pl. *indexes* or *indices)* or **index number** **(132-7)** is a ratio showing the value of a given quantity relative to a **base** **(132-8)**, which is usually taken as 100. Some indices are good **indicators** **(132-9)** of a complex situation; thus the infant mortality rate is sometimes used as an indicator of the health status of a population. - **132-1** **Analysis**, n. - **analytical**, adj. - **analyze**, v. - **132-3** **Calculate**, b. - **calculation**, n. - **calculator**, n.: a machine with minimal to modest data storage capabilities designed to facilitate a modest amount of arithmetic and statistical calculating.
**Compute**, v. - **computation**, n. - **computer**, n.: a machine system designed to effect the transmission, storage and calculations of large data sets; it permits arithmetic and statistical calculations as well as logical processing of data. In a dated sense, the terms calculator and computer were used to designate the person(s) engaged in the computations.
ctx_en.en:18:
One of the first stages of *analysis* (132-1) consists of relating the population totals or number of events to other totals or numbers. The resulting indices are given various names. A **ratio** **(133-6)**, also used for various purposes, is the quotient obtained by dividing quantities of the same kind. When the dividend and divisor belong to the same kind but different categories (men and women, children and women, different age-groups, for example) an other terminology might be used in non English languages, relating both quantities with a **specific ratio** **(133-1)** (like a sex ratio). A **proportion** **(133-2)** is a ratio which indicates the relation in magnitude of a part to the whole. A **percentage** **(133-3)** is a proportion expressed per hundred. A **rate** **(133-4)** is a special type of ratio used to indicate the **relative frequency** **(133-5)** of the occurrence of a particular event within a population or a sub-population in a specified period of time, usually one year. Although this usage is recommended, the term has steadily acquired a wider meaning and is often incorrectly used as a synonym for ratio (e.g. labor force participation rate, which is actually a proportion).
 - **133-2**  **Proportion**, n. - **proportional**, adj.
 - **133-4**  Rates are generally given per thousand, and where the term "rate" is used without additional qualification "per thousand" is generally understood. Some rates, however, are given per ten thousand, per one hundred thousand, or per million e.g. *cause-specific death rates* (421-10). On other occasions rates may be given per person or per hundred. The word "rate" is sometimes omitted, thus one may find the expression "a mortality of ten per thousand," but this is not recommended.
 - **133-6**  The *total fertility rate* (cf 639-4) is the sum of **age-specific fertility rates** (cf 633-9) over the age reproductive period and thus lost its inverse temporal dimension (per year). The difference is as important as between length and surface or velocity and acceleration. The term **synthetic index** (cf 132-5) is preferred in some languages to avoid the confusion with the inverse temporal dimension (per year) of a rate: number of demographic events divided by the time exposure or person-years. If used, the term **rate** in the expression ''total fertility rate'' refers to the implicit ''per woman'', which is not enough to qualify as a rate but enough for a dimensionless ratio.
ctx_en.en:19:
The *relative frequency* (133-5) of a non-renewable event is often regarded as an empirical measure of the **probability** **(134-1)** of occurrence of that event. This presumes that all the individuals who appear in the denominator have been **exposed to risk** **(134-3)** in some way, i.e. there must have been a **chance** **(134-2)** or **risk** **(134-2)** that the event in question could happen to them. The use of the term "risk" does not imply that the event in question is in any way unwanted; thus the term "risk of marriage" is used. The population is often divided into different sub-groups, in which the risk of the event in question is less variable between individuals than in the population as a whole; the subgroup is more **homogeneous** **(134-4)** with respect to the risk than the relatively **heterogeneous** **(134-5)** whole population. Rates calculated for such subgroups are called **specific rates** **(134-6)** as opposed to *crude rates* (136-8) which apply to the population as a whole. **General rates** **(134-7)** sometimes involve an age restriction, as in the instance of *general fertility rates* (633-8).
 - **134-1**  **Probability**, n. - **probable**, adj.
 - **134-4**  **Homogeneous**, adj. - **homogeneity**, n.
 - **134-5**  **Heterogeneous**, adj. - **heterogeneity**, n.
ctx_en.en:20:
**Age-specific rates** **(135-1)** are computed for single years of age or for age groups (**age-group specific rate** **(135-2)** or **age group-specific rate** **(135-2)**). **Duration-specific rates** **(135-3)** take into account the time elapsed since a **baseline event** **(135-4)** or **event-origin** **(135-4)** such as marriage or a previous birth. **Central rates** **(135-10)** are obtained by dividing the number of events during a year, or some other period (often five years) either by the **average population** **(135-6)** or **mid-year population** **(135-6)** or by the number of **person-years** **(135-7)** of exposure to the event in question during that year or period; the number of person-years is the sum, expressed in years, of the exposure time for all individuals in the observed group, over the year or period. The term rate is sometimes used also for another type of measure, obtained by dividing the number of non-renewable events in a year or a period of years by the size of the cohort considered at the beginning of the year or period; this measure is sometimes called an **attrition probability** **(135-5)** or more simply a **probability** **(135-5)**, and contrasted with the *central rate*, defined earlier. In this paragraph, the word "period" has referred to a length of time. In the expression **period rates** **(135-8)**, however, the word is used in its chronological meaning and refers to a specific calendar year or group of years; it is opposed to **cohort rate** **(135-9)** or **generation rate** **(135-9)**.
 - **135-5**  The word **quotient**, used in French for this type of rate, has sometimes been used in English.
ctx_en.en:21: Data are called **provisional** **(136-1)** if they are based on incomplete or insufficiently controlled observations. They are replaced by **final** **(136-2)** data when the observations are complete. Rates based on such data are called **provisional rates** **(136-3)** and **final rates** **(136-4)** respectively. Where information becomes available after figures have already been published, **revised rates** **(136-5)** may be issued. The expression **corrected rate** **(136-6)** usually implies that defective data or inappropriate methods have yielded results which are either misleading or of limited value for the purpose in hand and that an effort has been made to correct this, e.g., correction for underenumeration, correction for migration, correction for seasonal movement. **Standardized rates** **(136-7)** or **adjusted rates** **(136-7)** are designed to make it possible to compare different populations with respect to a variable, e.g. fertility or mortality, where the influence of another variable e.g. age, is held constant. The term **corrected rate** **(136-7)** has been used by some demographers as a synonym for standardized rate. When the data do not permit direct estimation of the rates (small population, for example), the use of **standard rates** **(136-9)** (cf. 403-6 for example) computed from data of good quality and applied to the real population, provides an indirect estimation of the expected number of events which can be compared with the observed number of events. Unstandardized rates are called **crude rates** **(136-8)**. Although they may be used to measure actual trends, false inferences may result from their uncritical use when populations with different *structures* (144-4) are compared.
ctx_en.en:22: Demographic *indices* (132-7) will in most cases relate to a particular **period of observation** **(137-1)** ; this is true in particular of most *rates* (cf. 133-4). An **annual rate** **(137-2)** will relate to a period of twelve months. Where observations are collected for a number of years and then averaged, the term **mean annual rate** **(137-3)** or **average annual rate** **(137-3)** is often used for the result. Where rates are calculated for periods different from a year they are **converted to an annual basis** **(137-4)** through multiplication by an appropriate factor. **Instantaneous rates** **(137-5)** are sometimes computed; they relate to an infinitesimal period of time, cf. for instance the *instantaneous death rate* (431-4) or the *instantaneous rate of population growth* (702-5).
ctx_en.en:23:
The primary objective of *cohort analysis* (103-4) is the study of the **intensity** **(138-1)** and **tempo** **(138-2)** or **timing** **(138-2)** of demographic phenomena. The intensity of a phenomenon initiated by one *non-renewable event* (201-4) may be measured by either the **ultimate frequency** **(138-3)** of occurrence for the given event or by its complement. The ultimate frequency reflects the proportion of persons who would have experienced the event, in the absence of extraneous influences, during the existence of the *cohort* (116-2). The intensity of a phenomenon initiated by a *renewable event* (201-5) such as births or migratory moves, can be measured by the **mean number of events** **(138-4)** per person in the cohort, also in the absence of extraneous influences. Tempo or timing may be defined as the distribution over time within the cohort of the demographic events corresponding to the investigated phenomenon. The results of *cross-sectional analysis* or *period analysis* (103-5) are summarized by **period measures** **(138-5)** — as opposed to **cohort measures** **(138-6)** — which can be constructed in various fashions. A commonly used technique consists in attributing the observed rates pertaining to various ages or durations to a **hypothetical cohort** **(138-7)** or **synthetic cohort** **(138-7)** .
 - **138-3**  This ultimate frequency or its complement has received various names according to the phenomenon studied: *parity progression ratio* (637-7), *frequency of definitive celibacy* (521-1) ... It is best not to use the word proportion as part of these names, and to reserve it for observed proportions. For instance, the frequency of definitive celibacy must be kept distinct from the proportion single at a given age, as recorded in a census.
 - **138-4**  It is not unusual to give the same name to the observed *mean number of events* per person, and to the number that would have been observed in the absence of extraneous influences such as mortality. Distinct phrases should be used; for instance, the *number of children ever born* (637-2) can be distinguished from *cumulative fertility* (636-2). 
 - **138-5**  Because cross-sectional analysis and hypothetical cohorts were used before genuine cohort analysis, the names of period indices often seem to imply that they refer to a cohort. This usage may lead to apparent contradictions. For example, parity-specific birth probabilities may exceed one for certain years when many postponed births are made up.
ctx_en.en:24:
The **average** **(140-1)** or **mean** **(140-1)** most frequently used in demography is the **arithmetic average** **(140-2)** or **arithmetic mean** **(140-2)** which consists of the sum of a series of quantities divided by their number.. Where the term average or mean is used without further qualification the arithmetic average is generally meant. The **geometric mean** **(140-3)** or **geometric average** **(140-3)** is sometimes used when all observed values are positive. It is the Nth root of the product of N values. A **weighted average** **(140-4)** or **weighted mean** **(140-4)** is obtained when different items are given varying importance by multiplying each item by a particular **weighting factor** **(140-5)** or **weight** **(140-5)**. The **median** **(140-6)** is the value of the element which divides a **set** **(140-7)** of observations into two halves. The **mode** **(140-8)** is the most common or frequent value in a set of observations.
 - **140-1**  **Average**, n., can be used as an adjective. **Mean**, n., can be used as an adjective.
 - **140-5**  **Weight**, n. - **weigh**, v.
 - **140-6**  **Median**, n., can be used as an adjective.
 - **140-8**  **Mode**, n., **modal**, adj.
ctx_en.en:25:
The **dispersion** **(141-1)**, **scatter** **(141-1)**, **variation** **(141-1)** or **variability** **(141-1)** of a set of observations depends on the **differences** **(141-2)** or **deviations** **(141-2)** between its elements. Here only the most common **measures of dispersion** **(141-3)** are mentioned. The **range** **(141-4)** is the difference between the largest and the smallest values of a set of elements. The **interquartile range** **(141-5)** is the difference between the first and the third *quartiles* (142-2) and contains half the observations in the set. The **semi-interquartile range** **(141-6)**, also called the **quartile deviation** **(141-6)**, which is half the interquartile range, is often taken as a measure of dispersion. The **mean deviation** **(141-7)** or **average deviation** **(141-7)** is the arithmetic mean (140-2) of the positive values of the deviations of the individual items from the average, the **variance** **(141-8)** is the arithmetic mean of the squares of these deviations and the **standard deviation** **(141-9)** is the square root of the variance.
 - **141-9**  The common notation for the standard deviation is *σ*.
ctx_en.en:26: If a series of observations is arranged in ascending order, values which have below them a certain proportion of the observations are referred to as **quantiles** **(142-1)** or **order statistics** **(142-1)** . *The median* (140-6) has been previously mentioned. Other important order statistics are the **quartiles** **(142-2)**, the **deciles** **(142-3)**, and the **percentiles** **(142-4)** or **centiles** **(142-4)**, which divide the observations into four, ten and a hundred equal parts respectively.
ctx_en.en:27:
A variable is **continuous** **(143-1)** in a given interval when it can take on an infinite number of values between any two points contained in the interval. In the opposite case it is said to be **discontinuous** **(143-2)**. Where a variable can take only certain isolated values it is called a **discrete** **(143-3)** variable.
 - **143-1**  **Continuous**, adj. - **continuity**, n.
 - **143-2**  **Discontinuous**, adj. - **discontinuity**, n.
ctx_en.en:28:
The arrangement of members of a population in various categories or classes of a specified attribute or variable produces a **frequency distribution** **(144-1)**, often called a **distribution** **(144-1)** for short. The ratio of the number in the individual group or cell — the **absolute frequency** **(144-2)** or **class frequency** **(144-2)** — to the total number in all groups is called the **relative frequency** **(144-3)** in that group. In demography the terms **structure** **(144-4)** and **composition** **(144-4)** are often used interchangeably to describe the distribution of characteristics such as age, sex, marital status, occupation, etc. Structure is sometimes used in a more restricted sense to describe the distribution of the population according to age and sex only.
 - **144-4**  The term *population distribution* usually refers to its spatial distribution. However, when used with the name of the characteristic or attribute that is analyzed, the word distribution is a synonym for structure or composition. Thus one finds references to age distribution, age and sex composition, and age and sex structure.
ctx_en.en:29:
When values of a demographic variable are available over time, a demographic **time series** **(150-1)** is obtained. It is sometimes possible to decompose a time series into a **trend** **(150-2)** around which there are **fluctuations** **(150-3)**, **variations** **(150-3)**, or **deviations** **(150-3)** (141-2). Where such fluctuations tend to recur after certain periods, usually several years, they are called **cyclical fluctuations** **(150-4)** or, more generally, **period fluctuations** **(150-4)**. In demography the most common period for compiling data is a year, and the fluctuations in sub-periods of a year are called **seasonal fluctuations** **(150-5)**. The fluctuations that remain after trend, cyclical, and seasonal fluctuations have been eliminated are called **irregular fluctuations** **(150-6)**. They may be due to exceptional factors such as wartime mobilization, or sometimes they are **chance fluctuations** **(150-7)** or **random fluctuations** **(150-7)**. 
 - **150-3**  In a general sense the term **variation** may be used to describe change in any value or set of values for a variable.
 - **150-4**  **Periodic**, adj. - **period**, n. - **periodicity**, n. **cyclical**, adj. - **cycle**, n.
 - **150-7**  **Random**, adj.: due to chance (cf. 161-1).
ctx_en.en:30:
It is occasionally desirable to replace a series of figures by another series that shows greater regularity. This process is known as **graduation** **(151-1)** or **smoothing** **(151-1)**, and it generally consists of passing a smooth curve through a number of points in the time series or other series, such as the number of persons distributed by reported age. If a free-hand curve is drawn the process is called **graphic graduation** **(151-2)**. When analytical mathematical methods are used, this is called **curve fitting** **(151-3)**. A mathematical curve is fitted to the data, possibly by the **method of least squares** **(151-4)**, which minimizes the sum of the squares of the differences between the original and the graduated series. Other methods include **moving averages** **(151-5)** or involve the use of the **calculus of finite differences** **(151-6)**. Some of these procedures may be used for **interpolation** **(151-7)**, the estimation of values of the series at points intermediate between given values, or for **extrapolation** **(151-8)**, the estimation of values outside of the range for which it was given.
 - **151-1**  **Graduation**, n. - **graduate**, v. - **graduated**, adj. **Smoothing**, n. - **smooth**, v. - **smoothed**, adj.
 - **151-7**  **Interpolation**, n. - **interpolate**, v. - **interpolated**, adj.
 - **151-8**  **Extrapolation**, n. - **extrapolate**, v. - **extrapolated**, adj.
ctx_en.en:31: It is often necessary to graduate distributions to correct the tendency of people to give their replies in **round numbers** **(152-1)**. **Heaping** **(152-2)** or **digit preference** **(152-2)** can be found in various duration distributions (e.g., distribution of marriage duration, breastfeeding duration or birth intervals), but is particularly frequent in age distributions and reflects a tendency for people to state their ages in numbers ending with 0, 5, or other preferred digits, but . **Age heaping** **(152-3)** is sometimes measured with **indices of age preference** **(152-4)**. Age data must often be corrected for other forms of **age misreporting** **(152-5)** or **age reporting bias** **(152-5)**
ctx_en.en:32: The numerical values of demographic functions are generally listed in **tables** **(153-1)**, such as *life tables* (431-1), *fertility tables* (634-1), or *nuptiality tables* (522-1). A distinction is usually made between **calendar-year tables** **(153-2)** or **period tables** **(153-2)** which are based upon observations collected during a limited period of time, and **cohort tables** **(153-3)** or **generation tables** **(153-3)** which deal with the experience of a cohort throughout its lifetime. A **multiple decrement table** **(153-4)** illustrates the simultaneous effects of several non-renewable events, such as the effects of first marriage and death on the single population. The most used are **double decrement tables** **(153-4)**. **Forecast tables** **(153-5)** provide numerical values of demographic functions, like *survival functions* (431-6) for example, which can be used directly for *population forecast* (cf. 720-2). When a population is classified in two or more categories according to age, like economic status (women in the labor force or out of the labor force, for example), marital statuses, regions etc. and when continuous flows between categories are possible over time even if the individual state can usually be measured only at discrete times (waves of a longitudinal study, queries to population registers etc.), **increment-decrement methods** **(153-6)** or **multi-state methods** **(153-6)** are more appropriate.
ctx_en.en:33: Where insufficient data exist to establish the value of a given variable accurately, attempts may be made to **estimate** **(154-1)** this value. The process is called **estimation** **(154-2)** and the resulting value an **estimate** **(154-3)**. Where data are practically non-existent a **conjecture** **(154-4)** may sometimes be made to establish the variable’s **order of magnitude** **(154-5)** .
ctx_en.en:34: Methods of **graphic representation** **(155-1)** or **diagrammatic representation** **(155-1)** may be used to illustrate the data. The data are represented in a **figure** **(155-2)**, **graph** **(155-2)**, **statistical chart** **(155-3)** or **map** **(155-3)**. A schematic representation of the relationships between variables is often called a **diagram** **(155-4)**, for example the *Lexis Diagram* (cf. 437). A graph in which one co-ordinate axis is graduated logarithmically and the other arithmetically is called a **semi-logarithmic graph** **(155-5)**, though such graphs are often inaccurately referred to as **logarithmic graphs** **(155-5)**. A **true logarithmic graph** **(155-6)** has both axes graduated logarithmically and is sometimes referred to as a **double logarithmic graph** **(155-6)**. A frequency distribution may be represented graphically by **frequency polygons** **(155-7)** obtained by joining points representing class frequencies with straight lines, by a **histogram** **(155-8)**, where class frequencies are represented by the area of a rectangle with the class interval as its base, by **bar charts** **(155-9)**, in which the class frequencies are proportionate to the length of a bar or by an **ogive** **(155-10)** representing the cumulative frequency distribution.
ctx_en.en:35: **Sampling procedures** **(160-1)** are used to obtain information about a population from part of the population only, instead of having to study *every person* (110-2). The part of the population studied is called a **sample** **(160-2)**. A population is a collection of **elements** **(160-3)** which are the object of the investigation. A **sampling unit** **(160-4)** may be an element or a group of elements of the population and is used for selecting samples. In demographic samples the elements are usually *individuals* (110-2), *families* (115-1), or *households* (110-3) and sampling units may be individuals, households, blocks of houses, municipalities or areas. The sample will consist of a number of sampling units selected in accordance with a **sampling scheme** **(160-5)** or **sampling plan** **(160-5)**.
ctx_en.en:36:
A sample whose elements are selected by a chance process is referred to as a **random sample** **(161-1)** or **probability sample** **(161-1)**. If a complete list of sampling units is available, this is called a **sampling frame** **(161-3)**. In **simple random sampling** **(161-4)** a proportion of sampling units is selected from the frame at **random** **(161-2)**. This proportion is called the **sampling fraction** **(161-5)** or **sampling ratio** **(161-5)**. **Systematic samples** **(161-6)** are **drawn systematically** **(161-7)** from a frame in which the sampling units are consecutively numbered. The sample is selected by taking the *n*<sup>th)**, (*n* + *s*)<sup>th)**, (n + 2s)<sup>th)**, ..., etc. unit, where *n* is not larger than *s* and is selected at random. In **cluster sampling** **(161-8)** population elements are not drawn individually, but in groups which are called **clusters** **(161-9)** .
 - **161-2**  **Random**, adj. - **randomness**, n. - **randomize**, v,
ctx_en.en:37:
In **stratified random sampling** **(162-1)** the population is divided into a number of **strata** **(162-2)** which are in some sense more *homogeneous* (134-4) than the population as a whole with respect to the characteristics studied, and a simple random sample (161-4) is drawn in each stratum. Variable *sampling fractions* (161-5) may be used in the different strata. **Multi-stage sampling** **(162-3)** is a method where the selection of the sample is carried out in several stages. A sample of **primary units** **(162-4)** is first selected and each of these units is then regarded as a population (101-3) from which a **sub-sample** **(162-5)** of **secondary units** **(162-6)** is selected, and the process may be repeated. When there is no good sampling frame, a sample of areas delimited on a map may be selected: this procedure is called **area sampling** **(162-7)**.
 - **162-1**  **Stratify**, v,: divide into strata (plural of stratum) - **stratification**, n.
ctx_en.en:38: In *probability sampling* (161-1), chance methods are used to obtain a **representative sample** **(163-1)** i.e., a sample which is a faithful reflection of the population with respect to all the characteristics under investigation except for random fluctuation. In **quota sampling** **(163-2)**, on the other hand, the sample is purposely selected so as to reflect the population in certain characteristics, and each *interviewer* (204-2) is given a **quota** **(163-3)** of different types of sampling units which are to be included in his/her sample. Within the limits of the quota the interviewer is free to select the sampling units.
ctx_en.en:39: A **population parameter** **(164-1)** is a numerical value that characterizes a population. **Statistical estimation** **(164-2)** is the name given to the procedure by which the values of such parameters are estimated from the sample. Such estimates are subject to **sampling errors** **(164-3)** and a measure of the magnitude of the sampling error is generally given by the **standard error** **(164-4)**. Sometimes a **confidence interval** **(164-5)** is associated with an estimate to show the limits within which the estimated quantity may be expected to lie with a pre-determined probability. A difference between two values is referred to as a **significant difference** **(164-6)** when the probability that it is due to chance is less than a given value which is called the **level of significance** **(164-7)**. Thus a difference would be significant at the 5 percent level if the probability that it could have arisen by chance is less than 0.05. In addition to sampling errors, **observation errors** **(164-8)** or **response errors** **(164-8)** also affect estimates. These errors usually include **interviewer biases** **(164-9)** which are systematic errors introduced by the interviewers when the basic data are collected.
ctx_en.en:40: **Current population statistics** **(201-1)** may be distinguished from **statistics of population change** **(201-2)**. They deal with the static aspects of the subject and give an instantaneous picture of the population at a given moment of time: the *statistical units* (110-1) used are generally *households* (110-3), *individuals* (110-2), etc. Statistics of population change are concerned with the continuous processes of change which affect a population, and deal largely with **vital events** **(201-3)**,such as births, marriages, deaths, and with migration (801-1). **Nonrenewable events** **(201-4)** (e.g. deaths) may be distinguished from **renewable events** **(201-5)** such as pregnancies, births or migratory moves; renewable events are assigned an **order** **(201-6)** based on the number of previous events of the same nature for the same person. Statistics of population change are a principal source for the study of **population processes** **(201-7)**, sometimes called **population dynamics** **(201-7)**. *Censuses* (cf. *202*) are the main source of information on the **state of the population** **(201-8)** . *Vital Statistics* (212-1) are the primary source of data for the study of **population growth** **(201-9)** (cf. *701*). Occasionally they deal with **natural increase** **(201-10)** only, i.e. they do not take into account movement between the population studied and other populations, but logically *migration statistics* (812-1) are a part of the statistics of population change. The term **population movement** **(201-11)** is used to refer to the geographical movement of a population.
ctx_en.en:41:
**Population censuses** **(202-1)** are taken to obtain information about the *state of the population* (201-8) at a given time. Most commonly all inhabitants of a particular country are counted simultaneously:. the census is then called a **general census** **(202-2)** Occasionally, however, only a section of the population is counted, e.g. the inhabitants of a given area, in which case the census is called a **partial census** **(202-3)**. The term "Census", however, denotes that an attempt was made to enumerate every member of the population concerned and to achieve **complete coverage** **(202-4)** of the population. A **micro census** **(202-5)** is limited to a sample of the population, usually large in size, and belongs in the category of **sample surveys** **(202-6)**. Censuses or surveys are sometimes preceded by **pretests** **(202-7)** or **pilot surveys** **(202-7)**. To verify the accuracy and completeness of enumeration (230-2), a **post-enumeration check** **(202-8)** is performed using a **post-enumeration survey** **(202-9)**. - **202-1** **Census**, n. - **censal**, adj. The **intercensal period** is the time elapsing between two successive censuses.
Modern censuses correspond to what used to be called **head counts**. **Population counts** include any estimation procedure, however imprecise, based for example on the counting of *baptisms* (214-2) registered for a number of years, or of *hearths* (110-3) or even *parishes* (214-1).
ctx_en.en:42:
An **enumeration** **(203-1)** is any operation which is designed to yield a population total. It differs from a simple **count** **(203-2)** in that a **list** **(203-3)** is generally prepared. An **inquiry** **(203-4)** or **survey** **(203-4)** on the other hand, is generally an operation which is designed to furnish information on a special subject (e.g. the labor force) and which has limited aims. A **field inquiry** **(203-5)** or **field survey** **(203-5)** is an inquiry in which information is obtained by **personal interview** **(203-6)**. In **postal inquiries** **(203-7)** or **mailback surveys** **(203-7)** *questionnaires* (206-3) are sent out by post with a request to return them completed. A **retrospective survey** **(203-8)** focuses on past demographic events; in a **multiround survey** **(203-9)** those events that occurred since the previous survey are noted from the second round on. This type of survey should not be confused with a **call back** **(203-10)**, a term used to describe the instance where the interviewer is obliged to make several attempts to reach a respondent. In censuses, information may be obtained by either **direct interview** **(203-11)**, or by **self-enumeration** **(203-12)**. In the first method, also called **canvasser method** **(203-11)** the enumerator (204-2) notes the information provided by or about the respondents; in the second method, also called **householder method** **(203-12)**, the questionnaire is completed by the *respondents* (204-1) themselves. Self-enumeration may take the form of a **mail census** **(203-13)**.
 - **203-1**  **Enumeration**, n. - **enumerate**, v.
 - **203-2**  **Count**, n. - **count**, v.
 - **203-3**  **List**, n. - **list**, v.
 - **203-4**  **Survey**, n. - **survey**, v.
ctx_en.en:43:
Persons who answer questions in a *census* (202-1) or a *survey* (203-4) are called **respondents** **(204-1)** or **informants** **(204-1)**. Persons who *collect* (130-4) the information are called **interviewers** **(204-2)**, **field workers** **(204-2)** or **enumerators** **(204-2)**, the last term being usually reserved for persons collecting information in a census. Enumerators usually work under the control of **supervisors** **(204-3)** or **inspectors** **(204-3)**. *General censuses* (202-2) are usually taken by the **statistical departments** **(204-4)** of individual countries.
 - **204-1**  The term **interviewee** is sometimes used.
 - **204-4**  In the United States of America the office responsible for the census is called the **Bureau of the Census**; in England and Wales it is the **General Register Office**, in Scotland the **General Registry Office**; both are headed by a **Registrar General**.
ctx_en.en:44:
Censuses are usually **compulsory** **(205-1)**, i.e. *respondents* (204-1) are under a legal obligation to provide the required information; in this respect they are different from **voluntary inquiries** **(205-2)** (cf. 203-4), where the problem of **non-response** **(205-3)** may become important. This is particularly the case in *postal inquiries* (203-7), where it is often necessary to **follow-up** **(205-4)** the first questionnaire by a second, or sometimes by a visit. **Non-respondents** **(205-5)** are frequently divided into those who **refuse** **(205-6)**, i.e. who are unwilling to cooperate in the inquiry, and those who could not be found by the *interviewer* (204-2). The latter are counted as **absentees** **(205-7)** or **no contacts** **(205-7)**. The replacement of an unusable sample unit with another unit is referred to as **substitution** **(205-8)**. The **proportion of refusals** **(205-9)** in response to a given question is a useful index of the reactions of the respondents.
 - **205-6**  **Refuse**, v. - **refusal**, n.
 - **205-7**  **Absentee**, n. - **absent**, v. - **absence**, n.
ctx_en.en:45: The **forms** **(206-1)** used for the collection of information have a number of different names. The term **schedule** **(206-2)** is frequently used, especially the term **census schedule** **(206-2)**. Most of the *forms* are **questionnaires** **(206-3)**, particularly when they are designed for **completion** **(206-4)** by the respondents themselves. At other times, officials obtain **statements** **(206-5)**, or **particulars** **(206-6)** which they **extract** **(206-7)** from documents primarily used for non-statistical purposes. The questions are usually of two basic types: **closed ended questions** **(206-8)** in which a respondent replies by selecting one out of a limited number of responses listed on the questionnaire or **open ended questions** **(206-9)** to which the respondent may give a spontaneous answer.
ctx_en.en:46: A census *schedule* (206-2) may be an **individual schedule** **(207-1)** containing information relating only to a single individual, a **household schedule** **(207-2)** containing information relating to each of the members of the *household* (110-3), or a **collective schedule** **(207-3)**, **nominal list** **(207-3)** or **enumerator’s schedule** **(207-3)** on which the *enumerator* (204-2) enters successively data for all the persons he enumerates. There may be special schedules for the *institutional population* (310-7), which are called **institutional schedules** **(207-4)**.
ctx_en.en:47: **Census operations** **(210-1)** usually begin with the delimitation of **census areas** **(210-2)** and **enumeration districts** **(210-3)**. Enumeration districts in towns and cities may consist of one or several **blocks** **(210-4)**, a block being defined as a group of buildings around which it is possible to walk without crossing a street, or which are bounded by some obstacle, such as a railway line or a river. Most of the larger cities of several countries have been subdivided into statistical areas called **census tracts** **(210-5)** which may contain one or several enumeration districts.
ctx_en.en:48:
**Vital events** **(211-1)** may be defined as births, deaths, stillbirths, foetal deaths, marriages, adoptions, legitimations, recognitions, annulments, divorces and separations; in short all the events which have to do with an individual’s entrance into or departure from life together with changes in **civil status** **(211-2)**. Records of these events are generally called **vital records** **(211-3)**, or **registration records** **(211-3)**. For legal reasons vital events have, in many countries, long been the object of **vital registration** **(211-4)** or **civil registration** **(211-4)**. **Birth registration** **(211-5)**, **marriage registration** **(211-7)** and **death registration** **(211-9)** use special forms as **birth records** **(211-6)**, **marriage records** **(211-8)** and **death records** **(211-10)**; these are the most common types of registration documents. The person responsible for maintaining these registers is called the **registrar** **(211-11)**. - **211-4** **Register**, n. - **register**, v. - **registration**, n.
**Civil registration systems** are the descendents of *registers* (214-1) kept by religious groups. A register was originally a bound book in which one or several lines were devoted to an event Today individual records often take the form of **certificates**. They are separate documents for each recorded vital event.
ctx_en.en:49:
**Vital statistics** **(212-1)** or **registration statistics** **(212-1)** are obtained by processing the registration record or a **statistical report** **(212-2)** established at the time of registration. **Tabulations by place of residence** **(212-3)** of the mother or of the decedent are often regarded as more useful for demographic purposes than tabulations by place of occurrence.
 - **212-3**  In many countries, the **time of registration** of a birth may be markedly later than the **time of occurrence**.
ctx_en.en:50:
The *registers* mentioned in a preceding paragraph (cf. 211-4) are distinct from the **population registers** **(213-1)** of those countries which possess a system of **continuous registration** **(213-2)**. In these registers every member of the population or every family may be represented by a **card** **(213-3)**, and the register is **maintained** **(213-4)** or **updated** **(213-4)** through information which reaches it through the local registration offices and through registration of any **changes of residence** **(213-5)** (cf. 310-6). It is usually **matched** **(213-6)** with the census results and brought up to date at regular intervals by special **checks** **(213-7)**.
 - **213-3**  A card file is a collection of cards. In general, a **file** is a collection of records arranged in convenient order.
ctx_en.en:51: *Historical demography* (102-1) often uses documents which precede or anticipate the development of *civil registration* (211-4) and *nominal lists* (207-3) from censuses. **Parish registers** **(214-1)** or **parochial registers** **(214-1)** contain information on the religious close equivalents of vital events such as **baptisms** **(214-2)**, *religious marriages* (503-2), and **burials** **(214-3)**. For **chrisoms** **(214-5)**, **summary baptised infants** **(214-4)** who die at home prior to a formal church ceremony, only the burial record is available. Nominal lists contain information either on a portion of the population or more rarely on the whole population. They include the a **status animarum** **(214-6)** which are nominal lists of all parishioners, **lists of communicants** **(214-7)** and **confirmation lists** **(214-8)**, as well as administrative and fiscal documents such as **hearth tax lists** **(214-9)**, **taxation rolls** **(214-10)** and **military conscription lists** **(214-11)**.
ctx_en.en:52: Data are extracted from parish registers with the help of several types of event **forms** **(215-1)** or **slips** **(215-1)** . These include the **baptism form** **(215-2)**, **marriage form** **(215-3)** and **burial form** **(215-4)**. The names of the **persons of record** **(215-5)** (i.e. the persons being baptized, buried or getting married) are inscribed on these forms, and information is recorded about the parents and other persons such as the **godfather** **(215-6)**, the **godmother** **(215-7)** and the **witnesses** **(215-8)**. Other **anonymous rolls** **(215-9)**, **nominal rolls** **(215-10)** and **transcription sheets** **(215-11)** are also used for summary extraction of the data, either with or without the names of the subjects. *Family reconstitution* (638-2) makes use of *family forms* (638-1). Extant family histories or **genealogies** **(215-12)** that reconstitute the descendants of an individual or a family are, under certain conditions, a valuable source of information on the demographic characteristics of the selected families.
ctx_en.en:53:
The process of obtaining statistical data from documents not primarily designed for this purpose is called **extraction** **(220-1)**. In general, whatever its source, statistical information is subjected to **processing** **(220-2)** which may be **manual** **(220-3)**, **mechanical** **(220-4)**, **electronic** **(220-5)** or a combination of these modes. Manual processing involves no equipment more complex than the **desk calculator** **(220-6)**. Electronic processing uses *computers* (132-2*). Regardless of the mode of processing, certain **types of operations** **(220-7)** must be performed including **editing** **(220-8)** of the data, *tabulation* (130-6*) and *calculation* (132-2) and **table preparation** **(220-9)**. These operations are made more or less complex depending on the mode of processing which is selected.
 - **220-1**  **Extraction**, n. - **extract**, v.
 - **220-2**  **Processing**, n. - **process**, v. The terms to process information, data processing, are used widely.
 - **220-8**  **Editing**, n. - **edit**, v. In English, the term refers to an operation performed either on the basic document or on the machine - readable data, to correct inconsistencies or eliminate omissions. In French, edition refers to the stage of table preparation.
ctx_en.en:54:
Editing the data usually requires the prior **coding** **(221-1)** of a certain number of entries on the **basic document** **(221-2)**. The **coding scheme** **(221-3)** establishes a correspondence between an entry and its translation into numeric or alphabetic codes. The code book collects and describes the coding schemes used with a particular set of basic documents. A coding scheme is usually designed to facilitate later groupings of the data. In contrast, a **classification** **(221-4)** is a mere list of individual codes where each **heading** **(221-5)** is given one or several numbers. After the data have been coded, they constitute a *file* (213-3*) which can be converted to machine readable form. The second stage in the editing consists in the **cleaning** **(221-6)** of the file, through elimination of errors by **validity checks** **(221-7)** and **consistency checks** **(221-7)**; these can be internal checks within each *statistical unit* (cf. 110-1) or may result from the comparison of different units. After errors have been identified, they may be corrected in the original document or the file by some automatic procedure.
 - **221-1**  **Code**, n. - **code**, v. - **coding**, n.
ctx_en.en:55:
The edited data are rarely used directly; they are subjected to *grouping* (130-7) and *tabulation* (130-6*), and this normally leads to a presentation in the form of *statistical tables* (131-4). These may be the outcome of **sorting** **(222-1)**, either manual or mechanical, resulting in the reorganization of the elements in a set according to predetermined rules, or more simply of a systematic count of the elements presenting a selected characteristic. The choice of elements or of characteristics may be based on the values of one or several quantitative attributes, or on the **modalities** **(222-2)** of one or several qualitative attributes. Few studies can do without computation, simple or complex, isolated or repetitive, and the *computer* (225-2) now allows calculation that would have been too lengthy by hand. These capabilities have led to the development of techniques of **data analysis** **(222-3)**. Deterministic and stochastic *models* (cf. *730*) often require considerable computations, and so do *simulations* (730-6).
 - **222-1**  **Sorting**, n. - **sort**, v.
ctx_en.en:56: The stage of *table preparation* (220-9) aims at making the results of processing conveniently available in the form of **listings** **(223-1)**, *numerical tables* (131-4) or *charts* (155-2), all of which are commonly used in **descriptive statistics** **(223-2)**. The use of **computer graphing** **(223-3)** and **computer cartography** **(223-3)** permits the mass production of graphical presentation.
ctx_en.en:57: Purely *mechanical processing* (220-4) did not involve the use of **electronic equipment** **(224-1)** which has come to replace the earlier **tabulating machines** **(224-2)** or **unit record machines** **(224-2)** and is much more versatile.\n - **224-3** **Punch cards** or **punched cards**.\n - **224-4** **Keypunch** or **card punch**.
ctx_en.en:58: Demographic research depends heavily on **electronic data processing** **(225-1)** using the **computer** **(225-2)**. The term **hardware** **(225-3)** refers to the physical component, whereas **software** **(225-4)** supplies the **user** **(225-5)** with ways to have access to the computer. **Computer specialists** **(225-6)** include **programmers** **(225-7)** who write **programs** **(225-8)** conceived by **system analysts** **(225-9)**.
ctx_en.en:59: The *hardware* (225-3) components of a *computer* (225-2) include one or several **central processing units** **(226-1)**, a **central memory** **(226-2)**, one or more **mass storage devices** **(226-3)** which use **magnetic tapes** **(226-4)** or **disks** **(226-5)** and a set of **input-output devices** **(226-6)**. The *software* (225-4) components include the **operating system** **(226-7)**, which has the task of efficiently managing the available **facilities** **(226-8)** for the *users* (225-5) running the **users’ programs** **(226-9)** and the **processing programs** **(226-10)** which are preestablished *programs* (225-8) designed for the solution of standard problems.
ctx_en.en:60:
A *user* (225-5) can process his problem by writing a *program* (225-8) in a general **programming language** **(227-1)** such as Fortran, Cobol, Basic or Algol, or a specific language, designed to use the *processing programs* (226-9) stored in the *central memory* (226-2) of the computer such as a **data base management system** **(227-2)** used to create and maintain a **data bank** **(227-2)**, a **survey processing program** **(227-3)** or a **statistical package** **(227-4)**. The devices which are used to enter and receive information from the computer can differ according to the mode of processing. In **batch processing** **(227-7)**, the normal input and output units are the **card reader** **(227-5)** and the **line printer** **(227-6)**. A **console** **(227-8)** is the normal input and output unit for processing in a **timesharing mode** **(227-9)**. In either instance the entry units may be spatially separated from the computer and processing under these conditions is accomplished by **remote terminal** **(227-10)**.
 - **227-1**  In addition to *programming languages* as defined above, other types of languages can be used to manipulate the *operating system*; these are usually referred to as **job control language**.
ctx_en.en:61: Any information processed in a *computer* (225-2) undergoes three main phases. First, **data entry** **(228-1)** or **input** **(228-1)** which may be done by using an **on line** **(228-2)** device such as a *keyboard console* (227-8). Data which is already stored in the computer may be accessed from either *central memory* (226-2) or from one of the *mass storage devices* (226-3) and used as *input data*. This is part of the **data collection** **(228-3)** which goes from *extraction* (220-1) to the transcription on an electronic medium, through *validity checks* (221-7) and *consistency checks* (221-8) that can be made ​​during data entry when working on line. The second phase, *processing* (220-2), is divided into two main types: **numerical processing** **(228-4)** and **non-numerical processing** **(228-5)**. Statistical or arithmetic computations are normally the operations contained in the former while data manipulation operations are the focus in the latter. In a third phase, occasionally referred to as output phase, the **processed results** **(228-6)** or **output** **(228-6)** may be printed out on the *line printer* (227-6) or saved as a file on a *mass storage device* (226-3) for further processing. Results may also be diverted to a **plotter** **(228-7)** to obtain processed results in the form of a graph or a figure.
ctx_en.en:62:
The **accuracy** **(230-1)** of population statistics will depend among other factors on the **completeness** **(230-2)** of the count of individuals, groups or events on which they are based. **Omissions** **(230-3)** and **undercount** **(230-3)** tend to generate **underestimation** **(230-4)** while **multiple counting** **(230-5)** leads to **over-estimation** **(230-6)**. Additional sources of error include **misreporting** **(230-7)** of a characteristic such as age and **classification errors** **(230-8)**. Such inaccuracies are sometimes detected by **post-enumeration tests** **(230-9)** or **quality checks** **(230-10)**. Occasionally certain questions are not answered or insufficiently answered and this may lead to considerable inaccuracy, the incidence of which is indicated by the frequency of the class designated as **non-response** **(230-11)**, **not stated** **(230-11)**, **unknown** **(230-11)**,  **undeclared** **(230-11)**, **not specified** **(230-11)**, **poorly defined** **(230-11)** or **misspecified** **(230-11)** etc...
 - **230-1**  **Accuracy**, n. - **accurate**, adj.
 - **230-2**  **Completeness**, n. - **complete**, adj. The terms "complete" and "completeness" are used here to express the absence of omissions. The same terms may also be used to refer to coverage, as in 202-4.
 - **230-3**  The omission of some events from vital registration is called **underregistration**, and from a census or survey, **underenumeration**.
 - **230-5**  The expression **double counts** is often used in this sense.
ctx_en.en:63:
Population statistics are generally presented in terms of the **geographical distribution of the population** **(301-1)** or the **spatial distribution of the population** **(301-1)**, and also by *structure* (144-4). Each population lives in a given **area** **(301-2)** or **territory** **(301-2)** (305-6), and the study of the **geographical distribution** **(301-3)** or **spatial distribution** **(301-3)** deals with the way in which they are distributed over the territory.
 - **301-2**  **Territory**, n. - **territorial**, adj.
ctx_en.en:64: The territory (301-2) in which a population lives will generally be divided into **sub-areas** **(302-1)**. For administrative purposes it may be divided into **administrative areas** **(302-2)**, **administrative units** **(302-2)** or **administrative districts** **(302-2)** sometimes known as **legal divisions** **(302-2)** or **political divisions** **(302-2)**. Geographers on the other hand, may divide the area into **regions** **(302-3)** or **zones** **(302-4)** which may or may not correspond to administrative units. The term "region" or "zone" may be used in a number of different senses and the areas referred to may be of very different sizes. Thus one speaks of the polar regions, of climatic zones or of metropolitan regions. The terms **natural region** **(302-5)** and **economic region** **(302-6)** are used by geographers. The term **natural area** **(302-7)** is used in *human ecology* (104-5) to define an area occupied by a population with distinct characteristics.
ctx_en.en:65:
Administrative units differ from country to country and over time in the same country, so that the same word may cover different situations. Minor civil divisions include **townships** **(303-1)** and **parishes** **(303-1)**; major civil divisions receive names such as **states** **(303-2)** or **provinces** **(303-2)**, and intermediary units are often called **counties** **(303-5)** and **districts** **(303-6)**. In Canada, for example the main administrative divisions, by increasing order of size, are the **township** **(303-8)**, the **county** **(303-9)** and the **province** **(303-10)**. As another example, the main administrative division in France are now the **regions** **(303-2)** which correspond to the province and the **departements ** **(303-3)** which correspond to the **cantons** **(303-4)** in Switzerland where **districts** **(303-7)** and **circles** **(303-11)** are minor civil divisions.  In the United States, parishes are equivalent to counties which are the unit above townships and cities but below states.
 - **303-1**  **Villages**, **boroughs** and **cities** are other names sometimes given to the smaller administrative units. **Municipality** is a general descriptive term for minor civil division.
ctx_en.en:66:
A population may be **settled** **(304-1)**, **sedentary** **(304-1)**, or **nomadic** **(304-2)**, i.e., migrating back and forth within a given area and without fixed abode. Nomads who are in the process of becoming settled are called **semi-nomadic** **(304-3)**. Occasionally primitive peoples may have a territory allocated exclusively to themselves called a **native reserve** **(304-4)** or **reservation** **(304-4)**.
 - **304-2**  **Nomadic**, adj.- **nomad**, n.
ctx_en.en:67:
A **country** **(305-1)** is usually the territory (301-2) of a **people** **(305-2)** (cf. 333-3) or a **nation** **(305-2)**. Persons belonging to a nation share, in general, a common culture. A **state** **(305-3)** is a political body. The term may be used in two different senses: most commonly a state is a body possessing full sovereignty in its territory and over its inhabitants. However, a number of **federations** **(305-4)** of **federal states** **(305-4)** are divided into smaller units which are also called **states** **(305-5)** and whose sovereignty is not absolute (e.g. in the United States of America and Australia). The term **territory** **(305-6)** (301-2) is generally used for a geographical area, but it is occasionally used to denote a political unit which has been settled relatively recently. A distinction is sometimes made between **self-governing territories** **(305-7)** and **non-self-governing territories** **(305-8)**.
 - **305-2**  **Nation**, n. - **national**, adj.
ctx_en.en:68:
Within a *territory* (301-2), certain terms are used to describe different kinds of **conglomerations** **(306-1)** or **aggregations** **(306-1)** of population, sometimes known as **population aggregates** **(306-1)**, **population clusters** **(306-1)** or more generally as **localities** **(306-1)**. In rural areas, the smallest unit is referred to as a **hamlet** **(306-2)**, which generally consists of a very small collection of houses. A slightly larger conglomeration is the **village** **(306-3)** which is generally a small community and which may have a mainly agricultural population. A **town** **(306-4)** or **city** **(306-4)** is a larger conglomeration in which there are in general few people engaged in agriculture, but the point at which the transition from village to town or city occurs is difficult to specify and varies in different countries. The seat of government of a *territory* (in the sense of 305-1), is called its **capital** **(306-5)**. In a county, the place where the local government is situated is called the **county town** **(306-6)** or **county seat** **(306-6)**. Towns and cities may be further divided into **districts** **(306-7)** or **quarters** **(306-7)** and for electoral purposes into **wards** **(306-7)**. - **306-1** The term **agglomeration** is also used in this sense. See however 307-1. - **306-4** A very large town or city is sometimes called a **metropolis**, n. - **metropolitan**, adj.
**Town**, n. - **urban**, adj.
ctx_en.en:69:
Continuously built-up areas may arise through the coalescence of neighboring localities which, while retaining their administrative independence, may constitute one **agglomeration** **(307-1)**, containing a **central city** **(307-2)** and **suburbs** **(307-3)** with specialized functions. The terms **conurbation** **(307-4)** or **metropolitan area** **(307-4)** are generally employed to designate a number of different agglomerations which, though geographically contiguous, have retained their own individuality. In many cases, however, the term conurbation is used as a synonym for agglomeration. The fusion of conurbations and large cities leads to the **megalopolis** **(307-5)** or **metropolitan belt** **(307-5)** which may extend over a large area. **Metropolitan regions** **(307-6)** may refer to agglomerations which include the commuter belt. - **307-2** Another term used as synonym is **urban nucleus**. - **307-3** Other terms used as frequent synonyms are **satellite communities** and **suburban zone**.
**Suburb**, n. - **suburban**, adj. - **suburbanization**, n.: the process of rapid population growth in the suburban zones adjacent to a large city. Densely populated areas contiguous to large cities are occasionally referred to as the **urban fringe**, and the zone marking the transition between urban and rural settlement, as the **rural-urban fringe** or **exurbia**. - **307-4** Urban populations are often regrouped in **statistical areas** such as the **standard metropolitan statistical area** (United States), the **densely inhabited district** (Japan) or the **conurbation** (England).
ctx_en.en:70:
In census practice a distinction is made between the **resident population** **(310-1)** or **de jure population** **(310-1)** of a given area, which consists of the people who habitually live in that area, and the **actual population** **(310-2)**, or **de facto population** **(310-2)**, which is made up of the persons in the area on census day. In the resident population, **temporary absentees** **(310-4)** are included with those **permanent residents** **(310-3)** who are present in the area on census day; the actual population consists of residents together with **visitors** **(310-5)** or **transients** **(310-5)**. The two methods of enumeration will give different results even for the country as a whole. The place where a person lives is called the **place of residence** **(310-6)**. For administrative reasons, certain persons who live together in large communities (i.e. boarding schools, military persons in barracks, prisoners, etc. (cf. 110-5*) are often separately enumerated. These persons form the **institutional population** **(310-7)**. Special rules are used to enumerate **homeless** **(310-8)** or **persons of no fixed abode** **(310-8)**.
 - **310-6**  The term **domicile** is a technical legal term for **legal residence** and denotes the place where a person is legally deemed to **reside**. This may differ from his actual **residence**. In the United States of America, the *de jure* population is the population of **usual residence**. 
 - **310-7**  In the United States of America the term **institutional inmates** is reserved for persons living under care or custody in correctional institutions, hospitals for mental disease and tuberculosis, homes for the aged, handicapped and dependent or neglected persons; **other residents of group quarters** include such persons as students in college dormitories, or soldiers in military barracks.
ctx_en.en:71:
In many countries a **rural area** **(311-1)** is defined as an administrative district in which the population size is below a certain level (often taken as 2,000). Other areas are called **urban areas** **(311-2)**. The **rural population** **(311-3)** is the population living in rural areas, the **urban population** **(311-4)** that living in urban areas. Criteria for allocating the population of particular areas to the rural or urban sector respectively differ in different countries. Certain definitions of rural and urban population may lead to distinguish an intermediate category referred to as the **semi-urban population** **(311-5)**. - **311-3** **Rural**, adj. - **ruralization**, n.: growth in the proportion of persons living in rural areas.
Rural population should not be confused with *agricultural population* or *farm population* (359-2). - **311-4** **Urban**, adj. - **urbanization**, n.: growth in the proportion of persons living in urban areas.
ctx_en.en:72:
The **density of population** **(312-1)** or **population density** **(312-1)** is an index showing the relation between a population and the area in which it lives. The simplest **density index** **(312-2)** is obtained by dividing the total population by the area of the territory and is generally expressed as the number of persons per acre, square kilometre or square mile. The **scatter of the population** **(312-3)** depends on the type of **settlement** **(312-4)**, **grouped settlement** **(312-5)** or **dispersed settlement** **(312-6)**. Some writers have computed the **population center** **(312-7)** of a given area by the methods used to find the center of gravity in applied mathematics; each individual in the population is given an equal weight.
 - **312-1**  **Density**, n. - **dense**, adj.
ctx_en.en:73: Where the pattern of settlement of different populations is to be compared and other factors besides surface area are taken into account, **comparative density indices** **(313-1)** are sometimes computed. There are various such indices, among which we may mention the **density of population per unit of cultivable area** **(313-2)** and the **density of the agricultural population per unit of cultivable area** **(313-3)**. Occasionally these indices are based on the **cultivated area** **(313-4)** rather than the **cultivable area** **(313-5)**. The density may also be expressed as a relation between population and total economic resources; the **maximum potential density** **(313-6)** or **population carrying capacity** **(313-6)**, showing the relationship between resources and the maximum population that can be supported with these resources, may be considered. The concept of **optimum density** **(313-7)**, i.e., the density which will give the maximum real income per head with given resources, is used in population theory.
ctx_en.en:74:
The **sex structure** **(320-1)** or **sex distribution** **(320-1)** of the *population* is measured by the ratio of the total number of one **sex** **(320-2)** to the total number of the population or, more frequently, to the total number of the other sex. By convention, the male sex is usually considered in the numerator and we speak of the **masculinity** **(320-3)** of the population. The **masculinity proportion** **(320-4)** is the proportion of males in the total population. The **sex ratio** **(320-5)** is the ratio of the number of males to the number of females; it is usually expressed as an *index value* (132-7) i.e. the number of males per 100 females.
 - **320-3**  Occasionally, the numerator of this ratio relates to the female population, and the feminity of the population is measured.
ctx_en.en:75: The terms **males** **(321-1)** and **females** **(321-2)** are commonly used in demography in place of **men** **(321-1)** and **women** **(321-2)** to refer to persons of each sex at all ages including *children* (323-3). In a similar fashion the terms **male child** **(321-3)** and **female child** **(321-4)** replace **boy** **(321-3)** and **girl** **(321-4)**. The term man is also used in the general sense of **human being** **(321-5)**.
ctx_en.en:76:
**Age** **(322-1)** is another fundamental characteristic of population structure. Generally it is expressed in years, or years and months; in the case of very small children, it may be given in months and days, or in years and decimal fractions of years. Demographers usually truncate the age to the number of **complete years** **(322-2)** lived, and this is called **age at last birthday** **(322-3)**. Occasionally demographic statistics refer to the **age reached during the year** **(322-4)**. Where the fraction of the last complete year lived is counted as a whole year, as in some actuarial applications, we speak of **age at next birthday** **(322-5)**. **Stated age** **(322-6)** or **reported age** **(322-6)**, in a census or vital registration, is often rounded upward to the next integer especially when the next birthday is near. The term **exact age** **(322-7)** is used, particularly in life table calculations, to denote the time when an individual reaches his birthday. Census questions include either the date of birth, age at last birthday, or even simply age without further precision. When the knowledge of ages is not widespread, a **historical calendar** **(322-8)** may be used to estimate ages. This is a list of events with a known date that occurred during the lifetime of the respondents.
 - **322-2**  Thus, *age groups* (325-2) are usually expressed in completed years and the group aged 6-13 years includes the individuals whose *exact ages* (322-7) are comprised between 6 and 14 years.
ctx_en.en:77:
In demography, certain terms which have been taken from everyday language are used to denote different **stages of life** **(323-1)** or an approximate range of years. At the beginning of life comes **childhood** **(323-2)**. In general a **child** **(323-3)** is a person who has not yet attained puberty (620-2). In the very early days of life, the child is called **newborn** **(323-4)**. A **child at the breast** **(323-5)** or **nurseling** **(323-5)** or **suckling** **(323-5)** is a child who has not yet been weaned from its mother or from its nurse. The term **infant** **(323-6)** may be used to denote a child who has not reached its first birthday, though in colloquial language it may be applied to children. Children who have not yet reached the compulsory school age are called **pre-school children** **(323-7)**, a **school-age child** **(323-8)** is a child at an age at which it is customary to attend school.
 - **323-6**  **Infant**, n. - **infancy**, n.: the period of being an infant - **infantile**, adj.
ctx_en.en:78:
Childhood is followed by **adolescence** **(324-1)** or **youth** **(324-1)** which starts at *puberty* < 620-2). The terms **adolescents** **(324-2)** or **young persons** **(324-3)** are employed for men and women between childhood and **adult age** **(324-4)**. Those who have reached **maturity** **(324-4)** are called **adults** **(324-5)**. **Old age** **(324-6)** is frequently used to define the period of life during which most persons are retired. Persons above that **retirement age** **(324-7)** are called **old people** **(324-8)**, **the aged** **(324-8)** or **the elderly** **(324-8)**.
 - **324-3**  The term **youth** is also employed collectively. When used in the singular, it more frequently refers to a male. In the United States of America, **teenager** refers to persons in their teens, i.e., between 13 and 19 years.
 - **324-4**  **Maturity**, n. - **mature**, adj. - **maturation**, n.: the process of growing to maturity.
ctx_en.en:79: The age distribution of a population is either given by **individual years of age** **(325-1)** or by **age groups** **(325-2)**, which may be **five-year age groups** **(325-3)**, also called **quinquennial age groups** **(325-3)**, or **broad age groups** **(325-4)**, such as 0-19 years, 20-59 years, 60 years and over. Occasionally a population’s **age distribution** **(325-6)** or **age structure** **(325-6)** is given by classifying the population by **year of birth** **(325-5)**. Graphically an age distribution may be represented by a **population pyramid** **(325-7)** which is a *histogram* (155-8) showing the population by age and sex and so named because of its typical pyramidal shape.
ctx_en.en:80:
The **mean age** **(326-1)** of a population is the average age of all its members, the **median age** **(326-2)** is the age which divides the population into two numerically equal groups. When the proportion of old people in a population increases, we speak of the **aging** **(326-3)** of the population. An increase in the proportion of young people involves a **rejuvenation** **(326-4)** of the population. An **old population** **(326-5)** has a high proportion of old people, a **young population** **(326-6)** has a high proportion of young people or children. The term aging used above should not be confused with the technique used in population projection, which consists of **aging** **(326-7)** a population by applying *survival probabilities* (431-6) by age to determine the number of survivors at a later date.
 - **326-3**  Also written **ageing**.
 - **326-4**  The word **younging** is used by American demographers.
ctx_en.en:81:
Aging (326-3) of a population must also be distinguished from **individual aging** **(327-1)** or **senescence** **(327-1)**, and from an increase in the duration of human life or **increased longevity** **(327-2)** which is the result of improved standards of living and of medical progress. An individual’s **physiological age** **(327-3)** will depend on the state of his tissues and organs. In the case of children we speak of **mental age** **(327-4)**, which is defined as the age at which the attainments of the individual child as measured by certain tests can be performed by the average child. In studies of mental and physiological age, a distinction is made between these ages and chronological age measured by the time elapsed since the individual’s **date of birth** **(327-5)**. The ratio of mental to chronological age is called the **intelligence quotient** **(327-6)** (often abbreviated to I.Q.).
 - **327-1**  **Senescence**, n. - **senescent**, adj.
ctx_en.en:82: Inhabitants of a nation or state may be **subjects** **(330-1)** **citizens** **(330-1)** or **nationals** **(330-1)** of that state, who enjoy certain political rights, or they may be **aliens** **(330-2)** or **foreigners** **(330-2)** who are citizens of another state, or citizens of no state at all and called **stateless** **(330-3)**. The term “subject” used to have a servile connotation but has tended to lose it and is frequently taken as a synonym of citizen, though occasionally a distinction is made between a subject and a citizen. Citizens of a state generally possess the **nationality** **(330-4)** of that state. This term is nowadays used as a synonym for **citizenship** **(330-4)**, but in some **multi-national states** **(330-6)** a distinction may be drawn between **political nationality** **(330-4)** and **ethnic nationality** **(330-5)**.
ctx_en.en:83: Aliens may acquire the nationality of their country of residence by **naturalization** **(331-1)** and become **naturalized citizens** **(331-2)** of **naturalized persons** **(331-2)**. In some countries **certificates of naturalization** **(331-3)** may be **revoked** **(331-4)** and naturalized persons will then suffer **loss of nationality** **(331-5)**. Persons may occasionally have more than one nationality, and will then be said to possess **dual nationality** **(331-6)**. A distinction is sometimes drawn between **resident aliens** **(331-7)**, who habitually live in a country other than their own, and **alien visitors** **(331-8)** or **visiting aliens** **(331-8)**, who are there only for relatively short periods.
ctx_en.en:84:
Individuals born in the territory in which they live are called **natives** **(332-1)** of that territory. If their ancestors were among the original inhabitants of that territory, they are called **autochthonous** **(332-2)**, **indigenous** **(332-2)** or **aboriginal** **(332-2)** inhabitants; the last term is often reserved for primitive peoples. Statistics frequently distinguish between **native-** **(332-3)** and **foreign-born** **(332-4)** individuals.
 - **332-2**  **Aboriginal**, adj. - **aborigines**, n., pl.
ctx_en.en:85:
The term **race** **(333-1)** is generally taken to mean a group of persons with certain common physical characteristics which are hereditarily transmitted. In some census practice, the term is sometimes used more loosely, sometimes for a group of people bound together by a common culture or national origin, or even for people inhabiting a given territory. Another term which is sometimes used is **ethnic group** **(333-2)** and here again there is no uniformity in meaning. Ethnic group generally refers to a group of people with common culture, language, or religious traditions. An ethnic group may be a racial group. A **people** **(333-3)** (cf. 305-2) is generally a collection of persons who are linked by a common past or a common culture. Persons living is a given territory who exhibit notable difference from the majority of the population are called **minorities** **(333-4)**, e.g., **ethnic minorities** **(333-4)**, **national minorities** **(333-4)**, **linguistic minorities** **(333-4)**, or **religious minorities** **(333-4)**.
 - **333-1**  **Race**, n. - **racial**, adj. 
 - **333-1**  **Racism**, n.: theory that certain races are inherently superior to others; **racist**, adj.
 - **333-2**  **Tribe**, and **tribal group**, still used in certain contexts, tend to be replaced by "ethnic group".
ctx_en.en:86:
Individuals are sometimes distinguished by their **color** **(334-1)**, which is used loosely to refer to the apparent pigmentation of the skin. In some countries a distinction is drawn between **white persons** **(334-2)** and **colored persons** **(334-3)** sometimes called **non-whites** **(334-3)**. Mating between persons of different colors is sometimes referred to as **miscegenation** **(334-4)**. A person who is the issue of such a union is said to be of **mixed blood** **(334-5)** or **mixed parentage** **(334-5)**.
 - **334-4**  **Crossing** is sometimes used in that sense. It also refers to the change in racial self-identification of an individual between one date and another.
 - **334-5**  The issue of a white and a **negro** is called **mulatto**. In Spanish America the issue of a person of European extraction and an American Indian is called a **mestizo**. The issue of a person of European extraction and an Asian is sometimes referred to as an **eurasian**.
ctx_en.en:87:
