The population may be classified by the **language** **(340-1)** or **dialect** **(340-2)** habitually spoken. A distinction is drawn between an individual’s **mother language** **(340-3)** or **mother tongue** **(340-3)** which is the language spoken in his home in his earliest childhood, and his **usual language** **(340-4)**, which is the language customarily used by him. The distinction between the two is not always very easy among people who are **bilingual** **(340-5)** or **multilingual** **(340-5)**. The statistics that present information on these topics are called **statistics of language** **(340-6)**. - **340-1** **Language**, n. - **linguistic**, adj.
**Linguistics**, n.: the study of the nature, structure, origin and meaning of language and human speech. - **340-2** **Dialect**, n. - **dialectal**, adj. A dialect is a variety of language that is distinguished by its pattern of pronunciation, grammar or vocabulary. - **340-5** **Bilingual**, adj. - **bilingualism**, n.
ctx_en.en:88:
**Religious statistics** **(341-1)** divide the population by religious affiliation. A distinction is generally drawn between the major **religions** **(341-2)** and their principal **denominations** **(341-3)**, **rites** **(341-4)** or **sects** **(341-5)**. Persons who have no religion may describe themselves as **agnostics** **(341-6)**, **freethinkers** **(341-6)** or **atheists** **(341-6)**.
 - **341-4**  **Rite**, n. may also be used in the sense of a religious ceremony.
ctx_en.en:89:
The population is also often classified by **educational status** **(342-1)**. Individuals who can read and write are called **literate** **(342-2)**; those who have reached a certain age and cannot are **illiterate** **(342-3)**. Often completion of a particular grade or level of schooling is assumed to confer literacy. **Educational attainment statistics** **(342-4)** classify individuals by **grade attainment** **(342-5)**, **years of school completed** **(342-5)** or, more rarely, by **age at leaving school** **(342-6)**. Another type of classification is based upon the **diploma** **(342-7)**, **degree** **(342-7)** or **certificate** **(342-7)** obtained, and depends on the organization of **instruction** **(342-8)** in each country.
 - **342-2**  **Literate**, adj. - **literacy**, n. **Literacy statistics** are the part of **education statistics** that refer to the ability to read and write. The **literacy ratio** is the proportion of the population covered that is literate. Its complement is the **illiteracy ratio**.
 - **342-3**  **Illiterate**, adj. - **illiteracy**, n. A person who is able to read but not write may be called **semi-literate**, and such persons are sometimes classed with the literate and at other times with the illiterate population.
 - **342-4**  The *school-age population* (346-7) is often classifed by grade or **level of enrollment**, and attainment is then presented only for the population beyond normal school age.
ctx_en.en:90: The **education system** **(343-1)** includes all institutions, public and private providing instruction in a country. Where both types exist a distinction is made between **public education** **(343-2)** and **private education** **(343-3)**. After **pre-school education** **(343-4)**, it is usual to distinguish between three **levels of education** **(343-5)** which are in ascending order: **primary education** **(343-6)**, **secondary education** **(343-7)**, itself often divided into several **cycles** **(343-8)** or **tracks** **(343-8)**, and **higher education** **(343-9)**. The latter includes, among others and at different **levels** **(343-10)**, courses of study that lead to a **university degree** **(343-11)**. **Technical education** **(343-12)** or **vocational education** **(343-12)** may be offered either at the secondary or higher education level.
ctx_en.en:91:
Types of **educational institutions** **(344-1)** and their names are a function of each country’s particular educational system. *Pre-school education* (343-4) is offered in **nursery schools** **(344-2)** or **kindergartens** **(344-2)**. The institutions that offer the three *levels of education* mentioned above (343-5) are usually called respectively: **primary schools** **(344-3)** or **elementary schools** **(344-3)**, **secondary schools** **(344-4)** and **colleges** **(344-5)** or **universities** **(344-5)**; in addition to the latter, there may be various kinds of **professional schools** **(344-6)**. *Technical education* (343-12) is given in  **learning centers** **(344-7)**, **technical schools** **(344-8)**, **technical colleges** **(344-9)**, **technical institutes** **(344-10)** and **educational institutes** **(344-11)**.
 - **344-5**  The term **college** is used in a variety of senses; a **university college** is either an institution of higher learning which has not full university status, or it may be a constituent college of a university.
ctx_en.en:92:
A **class** **(345-1)** (cf. 130-8) is a group of **pupils** **(345-2)** with the same **teacher** **(345-3)** who meet in the same **class-room** **(345-4)** and are generally instructed simultaneously. A group of pupils who are at the same level of educational advancement are said to be in the same **grade** **(345-5)** in the United States of America, or in the same **class** **(345-5)** or **form** **(345-5)** (cf. 206-1), in Great Britain. The term **student** **(345-6)** is generally used for those receiving higher education, but is also interchangeable with “pupil” at the secondary level.
 - **345-2**  A **scholar** in Britain is generally a pupil or student who has been given a scholarship from public or private funds; the use of the term as a synonym for pupil is archaic. In the United States of America such a student would be called a **scholarship holder** or **scholarship student**.
 - **345-6**  A university student who has not yet taken his first degree is an **undergraduate**. A **graduate** (cf. 151-1*) in Great Britain is the holder of a university degree; in the United States of America the term may be used for anyone completing his studies at the university, high school, or even primary school. In the *U.S*., a **graduate student** is one who is pursuing a second degree, the equivalent of a **post-graduate student** in the British system.
ctx_en.en:93:
**Current school statistics** **(346-1)** may distinguish between the number of **pupils enrolled** **(346-2)** and the number of **pupils in attendance** **(346-3)**. A comparison of these two figures gives an **attendance ratio** **(346-4)**. **Compulsory education** **(346-5)** implies the existence of a range of ages where school attendance is obligatory by law. This makes it possible to specify the number of children of **school age** **(346-6)** or the **school-age population** **(346-7)** according to a legal criterion.
 - **346-4**  The **attendance ratio** is the ratio of pupils in attendance to pupils enrolled, whereas the **enrollment ratio** is that of pupils enrolled to the school-age population.
ctx_en.en:94: Other statistics concern educational progression. An individual progresses normally grade by grade, from the lowest class of elementary school, to the end of his studies. **Leaving school** **(347-1)**, where compulsory education is enforced, is exceptional during school age, barring illness or death. The **dropout rate** **(347-2)** is the probability of leaving school before obtaining a degree, either during the year or at the end of a grade, and it is constructed in the same way as a probability of dying in a life table; its complement to one is the **retention rate** **(347-3)**. Such rates can be used to compute a **table of school life** **(347-4)**, from which it is possible to infer the **mean length of schooling** **(347-5)**. At the end of the school year, pupils or students who do not terminate their studies, may either repeat the grade or move on to the next grade, with or without **change of track** **(347-6)**. According to the fate of these pupils or students at the end of the academic year, **proportion repeating a school year** **(347-7)** are established.
ctx_en.en:95:
A distinction is generally made between the **working population** **(350-1)** or **economically active population** **(350-1)** and the **unoccupied population** **(350-2)** or **economically inactive population** **(350-2)**. Generally speaking, the working population consists of those individuals engaged in **gainful activities** **(350-3)**. A gainful activity, or **economic activity** **(350-3)**, is an activity which contributes to the production of income. *Unpaid family workers* (353-5) are usually included in the economically active population. **Homemakers** **(350-4)** or **housewives** **(350-4)** engaged in unpaid domestic duties, students, retired workers, etc. are usually excluded. The members of the economically inactive population are sometimes referred to as **dependents** **(350-5)** (358-1) in the sense that they subsist on the product of the working population. (See, however, the different sense of this term stated in § 358). The ratio of the working population to the total population, usually computed with reference to a given sex-age group or other category, is called the **activity ratio** **(350-6)** or **labor force participation ratio** **(350-6)**. - **350-1** The terms **gainfully occupied population**, **gainful workers**, **labor force** are used as synonyms for working population and economically active population.
For statistical measurement of the working population, the gainful worker concept or the labor force concept may be used. According to the **gainful worker concept**, the working population is defined as being composed of those persons who have a gainful activity which they normally exercise. According to the **labor force concept**, it is defined as the group of persons who were working at a gainful occupation or wanting or seeking such work during a specified period preceding the inquiry.
ctx_en.en:96:
**Workers** **(351-1)** who make up the working population can be classified as **employed** **(351-2)** or **unemployed** **(351-3)**. Under the *labor force concept* (350-1 *), only persons who were actively **seeking work** **(351-4)** or are on temporary layoff during the specified period are usually counted as unemployed. It is important to distinguish between persons who have never had a job and **persons who are looking for their first job** **(351-11)** or **first-time job seekers** **(351-11)**. The **employed population** **(351-5)** consists of all those currently working for pay or profit. Among the economically active, a substantial portion of workers may be compelled by the economic conditions of the country or of the time, to perform less work than they would normally be able and willing to perform; in this instance, the terms **underemployment** **(351-6)** or **partial employment** **(351-6)** are used. **Marginal workers** **(351-7)** who only very occasionally participate in economic activity, are most often classified as not in the labor force under the *gainful worker concept* (350-1 *). The **employment to population ratio** **(351-8)** is the proportion of employed persons in the working age group (usually 15 to 64). **Inactive persons** **(351-9)** are those who do not accomplish any kind of professional activity neither are looking for any employment.  **Hidden unemployment** **(351-10)** or **labor reserve** **(351-10)**  includes people who, although not officially registered as unemployed, are looking for a private work as well as those who do not exercise nor are looking for a job but if some job opportunities arose to them, could respond.
 - **351-2**  **Employed**, n. and adj. - **employment**, n.: situation of an individual exercising an economic activity. **Employment** status refers to the classification as either employed or unemployed. 
 - **351-3**  **Unemployed**, n. and adj. - **unemployment**, n.
 - **351-6**  One refers occasionally to **underutilization** of the labor force. Under-employment and underutilization also sometimes refer to the situation of persons who perform below their level of qualification.
ctx_en.en:97:
The **occupational classification** **(352-1)** of the working population (350-1) shows its members grouped by **occupation** **(352-2)**. The similarity of the work done by workers, including the similarity of skills and training required are the main criteria used for grouping occupations into **occupational groups** **(352-3)** or **occupational classes** **(352-3)**.
 - **352-1**  For purposes of comparability, the **International Labour Office** has prepared an **International Standard Classification of Occupations**.
ctx_en.en:98:
The working population (350-1) is also usually classified by **work status** **(353-1)**. In this classification **employers** **(353-2)** are distinguished from **employees** **(353-3)** on the one hand and from **workers on own account** **(353-4)** or **independent workers** **(353-4)** on the other. The latter do not employ labor for pay, but they, as well as employers, may be assisted by unpaid **family workers** **(353-5)** or **family helpers** **(353-5)** who are usually distinguished as a separate group. A combination of occupational and status classifications may be used to construct **social status categories** **(353-6)**.
 - **353-1**  The classification by **status** (as **employer**, **employee**, etc.) is designated by many different terms in the censuses of various countries, including “**industrial status**”, “**states in employment**”, “**position in industry**”, “**class of worker**”, etc.
 - **353-2**  **Managers** are sometimes counted with employers though they are themselves employed.
ctx_en.en:99:
Various sub-groups of the category of employees (353-3) are sometimes distinguished. One such sub-group is **home workers** **(354-1)** or **cottage workers** **(354-1)**, who work in their own homes, sometimes for several employers. Among the employees a distinction is sometimes made between **manual workers** **(354-2)** and **non-manual workers** **(354-3)** or **clerical and office workers** **(354-3)**. Manual workers may be further sub-divided according to their **skill** **(354-4)**, with **skilled workers** **(354-5)**, **semi-skilled workers** **(354-6)**, and **unskilled workers** **(354-7)** being distinguished. **Apprentices** **(354-8)** are sometimes shown as a sub-category of employees.
 - **354-2**  Another type of classification of employees is that which distinguishes between **wage earners** who are paid daily or weekly and salaried employees who are paid monthly or at even less frequent intervals. The statistics of the United States distinguish four broad occupational categories: **white collar workers**; **blue collar workers**, including **craftsmen**, **operatives** and **non-farm laborers**; **service workers**; and **farm workers** (cf. *356*).
 - **354-7**  A **laborer** is an unskilled worker, who does physical work.
ctx_en.en:100:
Among the employees (353-3) a distinction is often made between the **managerial staff** **(355-1)**, who make policy decisions; the **executive staff** **(355-2)** who apply the decisions; and **supervisors** **(355-3)** or **foremen** **(355-3)** who direct the operative. Officials () are divided into **simple or lower service** **(355-4)**, mainly for positions of menial work(eg, administrative assistants, technical assistants), **middle service** **(355-5)**, mainly for positions requiring roughly the equivalent of a completed apprenticeship (eg, editors, administrative secretaries), **upper service** **(355-6)**, mainly for positions requiring a Bachelor's degree or its equivalent (administrative frameworks or technical) and **senior service** **(355-7)**, restricted to graduates holding a Master's degree or its equivalent. 
 - **355-1**  The term **executive** in the United States of America refers to a member of the managerial staff.
ctx_en.en:101:
Special classifications apply in agriculture. **Farmers** **(356-1)** or **farm operators** **(356-1)** are those who farm the land for profit; among them we distinguish between **farm-owners** **(356-2)**, who own their land, **tenant farmers** **(356-3)**, who rent it from a landlord, and **share-croppers** **(356-3)**, who give a portion of the crop in return for the use of land and livestock. **Agricultural laborers** **(356-4)** are persons working who are employed by farmers.
 - **356-2**  A **farm manager** who is salaried is generally classed as a farmer.
 - **356-3**  In Scotland a small farmer is sometimes called a **crofter**. A farmer with a very small farm is also known as a **smallholder**.
 - **356-4**  Agricultural laborers are of three general types: **fulltime agricultural laborers**, **day agricultural laborers**, and **seasonal agricultural laborers**. This last category often consists of **migrant laborers**.
ctx_en.en:102:
The working population may also be classified by **industry** **(357-1)** or **branch of economic activity** **(357-1)**. This classification depends on the nature of the **firm** **(357-2)** or **establishment** **(357-2)** that the individual works for. Generally importance is attached to the division of the population into **agricultural workers** **(357-3)** and **non-agricultural workers** **(357-4)**. **Government employees** **(357-5)** are sometimes, and **military personnel** **(357-6)** or **members of the armed forces** **(357-6)** are generally shown separately, but employees of public enterprises are counted as a rule with the rest of the industrial population. Industries are generally classified in three sectors, the **primary sector** **(357-7)** (agriculture, hunting, fishing and mining), the **secondary sector** **(357-8)** (manufacturing, construction and utilities), and the **tertiary sector** **(357-9)** (commerce, finance, transport industries, and service industries). In developing countries the **traditional sector** **(357-10)** is often listed separately and opposed to the modern sector of the economy.
 - **357-1**  For purposes of international comparability, the United Nations have prepared an International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities.
 - **357-5**  A **civil servant** is an *employee* (353-3) of the central government. An **official** is an employee of a public body but the term is occasionally used for salaried employees of large companies. A distinction is often drawn between **government employees** and **private workers**.
ctx_en.en:103:
The economically inactive population may be divided into **dependents** **(358-1)** (350-5) and **self-supporting persons** **(358-2)**. Dependents depend for their support on the efforts of **earners** **(358-3)** or **breadwinners** **(358-3)**; this is for example the case of *housewives* (350-4) and **dependent children** **(358-4)**. Self-supporting persons have sufficient means for their subsistence. They may be **rentiers** **(358-5)** or **persons of independent means** **(358-5)**, **retired persons** **(358-6)** or **pensioners** **(358-6)**. A special category of dependents is that of **persons receiving public assistance** **(358-7)** or **public welfare recipients** **(358-7)**. Persons incapable of work are called **unemployable** **(358-8)**. The ratio of the inactive to the active population is called the **economic dependency ratio** **(358-9)**.
 - **358-1**  **Dependent** or **dependant**, n. - **dependent**, adj. - **dependency** or **dependancy**, n.: the state of being dependent.
 - **358-9**  The ratio of the young and the elderly to the adult population is called the **age dependency ratio**.
ctx_en.en:104: It is possible to classify the population by the sector of economic activity from which they derive their livelihood, dependants being put into the same category as their breadwinners. We speak of the **population dependent on** **(359-1)** a particular branch of activity and in particular of the **population dependent on agriculture** **(359-2)**. The term **agricultural population** **(359-2)** is sometimes used as a synonym, but may also be employed in the sense of **farm population** **(359-2)** which lives on farms or is dependent on agriculture and which is distinguished from the **non-farm population** **(359-3)** or **non-agricultural population** **(359-3)**.
ctx_en.en:105: The **infirm** **(360-1)** or **handicapped** **(360-1)** are often separately shown in censuses. They are classified according to the nature of their **infirmity** **(360-2)** or **handicap** **(360-2)**. **Physical infirmities** **(360-3)** or **physical handicaps** **(360-3)** such as blindness, or deaf-mutism are generally distinguished from **mental infirmities** **(360-4)** or **mental handicaps** **(360-4)**, such as feeblemindedness or dementia.
ctx_en.en:106: The study of the **working life** **(361-1)** of individuals includes the study of the **accession to the labor force** **(361-2)** and of the **separation from the labor force** **(361-3)**. At accession it is possible to distinguish those who have never been active, from those who belonged to the labor force at an earlier date; separations may be listed by cause, e.g. death, **retirement** **(361-4)**, temporary withdrawal. The analysis may proceed by cohort or period, and it involves **rates of accession to the labor force** **(361-5)**, or **probabilities of accession to the labor force** **(361-6)**, **rates of separation from the labor force** **(361-7)** or **probabilities of separation from the labor force** **(361-8)**, eventually by cause; these indices are computed by age or age-group.
ctx_en.en:107:
These indices serve to compute **tables of working life** **(362-1)**, by period or cohort. In addition to the probabilities described in the previous paragraph, these tables contain the distributions by **age at accession to the labor force** **(362-2)** and by **age at separation from the labor force** **(362-3)**, (eventually by cause, before and after accounting for mortality), the **mean age at accession to the labor force** **(362-4)** and the **mean age at separation from the labor force** **(362-5)**. The **expectation of working life** **(362-6)**, the **gross expectation of working life** **(362-7)** (which excludes the effect of mortality) and the **net expectation of working life** **(362-8)** (which includes it) all represent the mean number of years of working life that remain to be lived at each age by the active population. For those entering the labor force at that age, this expectation constitutes the **mean duration of working life** **(362-9)**; a similar index can be computed for all ages at accession taken together.
 - **362-1**  Such tables are computed when temporary withdrawals from the labor force are a negligible proportion of the total, and this condition is approximately realized for males. For females, it is necessary to distinguish **first accession to the labor force**, or **entry into the labor force**, from **re-entry into the labor force**.
ctx_en.en:109: A multidimensional construct that links gender identity, gender expression, and social and cultural expectations about status, characteristics, and behavior that are associated with sex traits.
ctx_en.en:110: The gender that a person feels internally and individually.
ctx_en.en:111: A multidimensional construct encompassing emotional, romantic, and sexual attraction, identity, and behavior.
ctx_en.en:112: Population in ages considered economically productive, often ages 15 to 64.
ctx_en.en:113:
The study of **mortality** **(401-1)** deals with the effect of death on the population. The general terms **mortality rate** **(401-2)** or **death rate** **(401-2)** encompass all the *rates* (133-4) which measure the frequency of **deaths** **(401-3)**. Where the expression death rate is used without any qualifying adjective the **crude death rate** **(401-4)** is usually meant (cf. 136-8 for a general discussion of *crude rates)*. This is generally an annual rate and consists of the ratio of the annual number of deaths occurring during a calendar year to the number exposed to the risk of dying during the same period. This number is equivalent to the **mean population** **(401-5)** or **average population** **(401-5)** for the period, and the population at the mid-point of the period can usually be substituted for the average population without appreciable error, if the size of the population is changing fairly uniformly. If the mortality of a *sub-population* (101-6) only is studied, we speak of *specific death rates* (134-6) among which **sex-age-specific death rates** **(401-6)** are the most common. **Age specific death rates** **(401-7)** without distinction of sex are also used on occasion.
 - **401-2**  Occasionally the term **mortality** is used as a synonym for mortality rate or death rate.
 - **401-3**  **Death**, n. - **die**, v. - **dead**, adj. syn. - **deceased**, adj. or n.
 - **401-5**  When the observation period exceeds one year, the mean population is generally obtained as the average of several estimates of the size of the population for each year. The *average number of persons years* (135-6) is also used as denominator.
ctx_en.en:114:
Specific death rates may be used to study **differential mortality** **(402-1)** or **mortality differences** **(402-1)** between groups, and reference is made to an **excess mortality** **(402-2)** of one group as compared with another, or with the rest of the population. It is measured by an **excess mortality index** **(402-3)**. The study of differences in the death rates of specific occupations is called the study of **occupational mortality** **(402-4)**. In a rather different sense the term **occupational mortality** **(402-5)** may refer to the mortality from hazards associated with a particular occupation. Among these, we may mention **occupational diseases** **(402-6)**.
 - **402-1**  Differentials in mortality is also encountered.
 - **402-2**  The expression **excess male mortality** implies a comparison with the corresponding female mortality, e.g. at the same age.
ctx_en.en:115:
*Crude death rates* (401-4) will depend upon the structure [particularly the *age structure* (325-6)] of the population as well as on the level of mortality. If the mortality of different populations is to be compared **standardized mortality rates** **(403-1)** or **adjusted mortality rates** **(403-1)** are sometimes computed to eliminate the effect of differences in *population structure* (144-4). Age is the characteristic for which mortality rates are adjusted most frequently by reference to a **standard population** **(403-2)** with a given structure. If *specific rates* (134-6) for the population studied are available, it is possible to use the **direct method of standardization** **(403-3)** which consists of applying these rates to the corresponding groups of the standard population. If specific rates are not available, it is still possible to obtain standardized mortality rates by the **indirect method of standardization** **(403-4)**. More frequently, **comparative mortality indices** **(403-5)** are computed by applying **standard mortality rates** **(403-6)** to the different groups of the population studied and summing these to obtain an expected number of deaths; the indices are then obtained by comparing the **observed deaths** **(403-7)** in the population with the **expected deaths** **(403-8)** which would have occurred had the standard rates applied.
 - **403-1**  **Standardize**, v. - **standardized**, adj. - **standardization**, n.: the process of standardizing.
 - **403-5**  If a crude death rate (401-4) is multiplied by a comparative mortality index, we obtain an **indirectly standardized death rate**. In British official terminology, when occupational mortality is studied, the figure obtained by direct standardization is called a **comparative mortality figure** and that obtained by indirect standardization a **standardized mortality ratio**.
ctx_en.en:116:
The mortality of live-born children who have not yet reached their first birthday is called **infant mortality** **(410-1)**. The mortality of live-born children who die before reaching a certain age taken as four weeks or 28 days, the so-called **neo-natal period** **(410-3)**, is called **neo-natal mortality** **(410-2)**. The mortality during the first week of life and between the first week until before 28 days are called respectively **early neo-natal mortality** **(410-4)** and **late neo-natal mortality** **(410-6)**. The term **post-neonatal mortality** **(410-5)** refers to deaths after the neo-natal period, but before reaching the age of one year.
 - **410-3**  In certain statistics the neo-natal period is defined as the first month of life. The term **early infancy** is occasionally used as an approximate equivalent to the neo-natal period, as, e.g., in "diseases of early infancy."
ctx_en.en:117:
The expression **foetal mortality** **(411-1)** is used for deaths prior to the complete expulsion or extraction from its mother of a *product of conception* (602-6) irrespective of the *duration of pregnancy* (603-3). The terms **intra-uterine mortality** **(411-1)** or **mortality in utero** **(411-1)** may also be used. The corresponding deaths are called **foetal deaths** **(411-2)** or **intra-uterine deaths** **(411-2)**. **Early foetal mortality** **(411-3)** occurs before the twentieth week of gestational life, while **intermediate foetal mortality** **(411-4)** occurs between the twentieth and the 28th week of gestation. After the twenty-eighth week, one refers to **late foetal mortality** **(411-5)** and the product is called a **late foetal death** **(411-5)** or, popularly, a **stillbirth** **(411-5)**. **Perinatal mortality** **(411-6)** includes late foetal mortality and a portion of infant mortality that may include either early neo-natal deaths, or all neo-natal deaths. The **foeto-infant mortality** **(411-7)** includes stillbirths and deaths of children under one year.
 - **411-1**  **Foetal** - also spelled **fetal**.
 - **411-2**  Also designated as **pregnancy wastage**. These terms include *abortions* (603-5), *miscarriages* (604-1) and stillbirths.
 - **411-3**  Early foetal deaths are also popularly known as **miscarriages**.
 - **411-5**  **Stillbirth**, n. - **stillborn**, adj. In certain countries, including France, children born alive who died before registration may be legally included among the stillborn, and are called **false stillbirths**.
 - **411-6**  The corresponding deaths are called **perinatal deaths**.
ctx_en.en:118: The ratios of **deaths under one year of age** **(412-1)**, of deaths of less than 28 days, and of deaths of less than one week, occurring in a year, to the number of live births of the same year give respectively the **infant mortality rate** **(412-2)**, the **neo-natal mortality rate** **(412-3)** and the **early neo-natal mortality rate** **(412-4)**. These rates are generally expressed per one thousand live births. When deaths are cross-classified by age and year of birth, it is possible to divide the deaths under one year by the births in the two cohorts to which they belong. The resulting index is an **adjusted infant mortality rate** **(412-5)** equivalent to a **probability of dying before age one** **(412-5)**. In the absence of such information **separation factors** **(412-6)** may be estimated, which divide infant deaths into those occurring to infants born in the current calendar year and to infants born in the previous calendar year.
ctx_en.en:119:
The proportion of *late foetal deaths* (411-5) among all births is called a **late foetal mortality rate** **(413-1)**. The ratio of late foetal deaths to *live births* (601-4) is called a **late foetal mortality ratio** **(413-2)**. A **foetal mortality rate** **(413-3)** represents the number of known intra-uterine deaths per one thousand births in the same year while the **foetal mortality ratio** **(413-4)** is the ratio of intra-uterine deaths to live births in a given year. These indices greatly understate intra-uterine mortality since early intra-uterine deaths frequently remain unobserved or unknown. A better measurement of intra-uterine mortality is provided by **intra-uterine mortality tables** **(413-5)**, a specialized application of the *life table* (cf. *432*) which takes into account the duration of gestation. The **perinatal mortality rate** **(413-6)** relates *perinatal deaths* (411-6*) to the sum of late foetal deaths and live births. The **foeto-infant death rate** **(413-7)** represents the number of known stillbirths and deaths in the first year of life per one thousand live births and stillbirths of the same reporting period.
 - **413-1**  Also called **stillbirth rate**. This usage is not recommended.
 - **413-2**  Also called **stillbirth ratio**. This usage is not recommended.
 - **413-6**  The **perinatal mortality ratio** relates perinatal deaths to live births only.
ctx_en.en:120: In the study of **age-specific mortality** **(414-1)**, the terms *infant mortality* (410-2) and *neo-natal mortality* (410-3) refer to generally accepted time periods. The usage of such terms as **child mortality** **(414-2)**, **youth mortality** **(414-3)**, **adult mortality** **(414-4)** or **mortality of old age** **(414-5)** is not uniform. **Post-infantile child death rate** **(414-6)** sometimes refers to the death rate between one and 4 years of age.
ctx_en.en:121:
The study of **morbidity** **(420-1)** deals with the investigation of **illness** **(420-2)**, **sickness** **(420-2)**, **ill-health** **(420-2)** or **disease** **(420-2)** in a population. Two aspects are considered: the **incidence of disease** **(420-3)** and the **prevalence of disease** **(420-4)** according to whether the new **cases of disease** **(420-5)** are considered or the number of cases existing at one point in time. The compilation of **morbidity statistics** **(420-6)** is hampered by the lack of a sharp distinction between health and the **morbid state** **(420-7)**. **Nosology** **(420-8)** and **nosography** **(420-9)** contribute respectively to the classification and description of diseases.
 - **420-2**  **Disease**, **illness**, or **sickness** are used as collective nouns in the singular, or both in the singular or plural to designate specific **ailments**.
ctx_en.en:122: **Health statistics** **(421-1)** encompass morbidity statistics, but also cover all aspects of the health of a population, and are generally taken to include statistics of **cause-specific mortality** **(421-2)**. The classification of deaths by **cause of death** **(421-3)** is made difficult because in many cases there may not be a **single cause of death** **(421-4)** but **multiple causes of death** **(421-5)** or **joint causes of death** **(421-5)**. When this is the case we may distinguish between the **immediate cause of death** **(421-6)** and the **underlying cause of death** **(421-7)** or, looking at the problem from a different point of view, we may distinguish between the **primary cause of death** **(421-8)** or **principal cause of death** **(421-8)** and the **secondary cause of death** **(421-9)**, **contributory cause of death** **(421-9)** or **associated cause of death** **(421-9)**. The **cause-specific death rate** **(421-10)** is generally expressed per 100,000 population. The ratio of the number of deaths from a specific cause to the number of deaths from all causes is referred to as the **cause-specific death ratio** **(421-11)**. Such ratios calculated for specific age groups or the general population provide information of the underlying **structure of causes of death** **(421-12)**.
ctx_en.en:123:
Death or *disability* (426-2) may be the consequence of *disease* (420-2) or of **injury** **(422-1)** or **poisoning** **(422-2)**. Injuries may be due to **accident** **(422-3)** or **violence** **(422-4)**. Among cases of violence it is normal to distinguish **suicides** **(422-5)** and **attempted suicides** **(422-5)**, **homicides** **(422-6)** and **deaths or injuries due to operations of war** **(422-7)**.
 - **422-1**  **Injury**. A distinction is often made between intentional and unintentional injury.
 - **422-3**  **Accident**, n. - **accidental**, adj.
 - **422-4**  **Violence**, n. - **violent**, adj.
 - **422-6**  **Homicide**, n.: May in law be **murder** or **manslaughter**.
 - **422-7**  Abbreviated to **war deaths** and **war injuries**.
ctx_en.en:124:
An **endemic disease** **(423-1)** is one that permanently affects substantial segments of a population, in contrast with an **epidemic** **(423-2)**, which spreads and then disappears within a fairly short time; when it appears in a large number of countries, it is called a **pandemic** **(423-3)**. Certain **infectious diseases** **(423-4)** or **communicable diseases** **(423-4)** have attracted particular attention, because they are capable of infecting large numbers of persons within relatively short time intervals. In such instances we speak of **epidemic diseases** **(423-5)**, and special **epidemiological statistics** **(423-6)** are collected to show their incidence. It is possible to obtain information about these illnesses in various countries because legislation has made their reporting compulsory; they are therefore called **notifiable diseases** **(423-7)**. A distinction is sometimes made between **chronic diseases** **(423-8)** and **acute diseases** **(423-9)**. These terms are not precisely defined, but acute diseases are generally understood to be those of abrupt onset and short duration while chronic diseases are those with slow onset and long duration, and often causing prolonged disability.
 - **423-2**  **Epidemic**, n., also used as adj.
 - **423-4**  **Infectious**, adj. - **infect**, v. - **infection**, n. The terms **communicable diseases**, **contagious diseases** and **infectious diseases** are not synonymous. A contagious disease can only be transmitted from person to person; thus, malaria, a communicable disease, is not contagious. Moreover, certain infectious diseases are not communicable. 
 - **423-6**  **Epidemiology**, n.: the science dealing with epidemics - **epidemiologist**, n.: a specialist in epidemiology - **epidemiological**, adj.: pertaining to epidemiology. The meaning of these terms has expanded greatly, and epidemiology now covers the study of relations between a biological or medical phenomenon and various factors, such as tobacco for example in "the epidemiology of lung cancer," or alternatively the statistical analysis of geographic variations in health phenomena.
ctx_en.en:125:
Demographers devote particular attention to certain aspects of mortality: **endogenous mortality** **(424-1)** which results from the genetic constitution of the individual, **congenital malformations** **(424-2)**, injuries connected with birth, or degenerative diseases associated with aging; **exogenous mortality** **(424-3)**, in contrast, results from external causes such as infectious or parasitic diseases and accidental injuries other than those incurred by the child during birth. Also of special interest are diseases connected with pregnancy, labor and the **puerperium** **(424-4)**. Mortality from these latter diseases is called **maternal mortality** **(424-5)**, and a **maternal death rate** **(424-6)** may be computed as the ratio of maternal deaths in a year to the births of the same year. The proportion of deaths due to **senility** **(424-7)** has mostly drawn interest as an index of poor reporting of causes of death.
 - **424-1**  *Infant mortality* (410-1) can thus be decomposed into **endogenous infant mortality** and **exogenous infant mortality**.
 - **424-3**  See note 1.
 - **424-4**  The **puerperium** is the **lying-in period** following a birth, and the mortality of mothers during the period is called **puerperal mortality**.
 - **424-6**  **Maternal death rate** is an inappropriate, but commonly used, term for a simple ratio.
 - **424-7**  **Senility** n. - **senile**, adj.
ctx_en.en:126:
Three aspects of morbidity (420-1) are commonly measured by **morbidity rates** **(425-1)** or **morbidity ratios** **(425-1)**: frequency, duration and severity. These indices may be computed for specific diseases, or for all diseases. Two indices of the frequency of ill-health are the **incidence rate** **(425-2)**, the number of new cases of disease during the period related to the average population, and the **prevalence rate** **(425-3)**, the number of cases existing at a given moment of time expressed per unit of the average population. Either the **average duration per case** **(425-4)**, or the **disability rate** **(425-5)**, which is the **mean number of days of illness** **(425-5)** per person in the population, may serve as a measure of the duration of illness. The **case fatality rate** **(425-6)**, which is the proportion of fatal cases among the reported cases of the specified diseases, may be used as an index of severity.
 - **425-5**  **Disability rate** is an inappropriate, but commonly used, term for a ratio of the number of days lived with illness divided by the number of days lived by the entire population, both in the same time interval.
 - **425-6**  This is said to measure the **lethality** of the disease.
ctx_en.en:127: An **impairment** **(426-1)** refers to any physical, functional or psychological defect, which results from illness, injury or congenital malformation. When an impairment inhibits an individual’s ability to work or participate in normal activities it is referred to as **incapacity** **(426-2)** or **disability** **(426-2)**. This may be total or partial; in either case, **permanent disability** **(426-3)** or **infirmity** **(426-4)** refer to an irreversible condition which gives rights to **professional incapacity** **(426-7)** or **work incapacity** **(426-8)** compensations. The probability that a healthy individual aged exactly x years will become disabled in the next year or over the course of some number of years starting with this exact age, is called the **risk of disability** **(426-5)** or the **probability of disability** **(426-5)**. A series of these probabilities can be combined into a **disability table** **(426-6)**, which is a specialized extension of the *life table* (cf. §432).
ctx_en.en:128:
Mortality statistics are generally compiled from death registration (cf. *211*). When a death takes place a **death certificate** **(430-1)** is generally issued; statistics are compiled from the information given on death certificates. In some countries a distinction is made between the **medical certificate of death** **(430-2)** issued by a medical practitioner who has attended the deceased person at the time of his/her death, and an ordinary death certificate issued by the registrar of deaths for legal purposes.
 - **430-1**  The first death statistics in England and Wales were compiled from **bills of mortality** which were generally drawn up on the basis of **burial registers**. In countries where vital registration is deficient, statistics can be gathered by the survey technique; questions may be asked on deaths during a reference period, generally the previous year; the **indirect estimation of mortality** relies on such questions as the **number of children surviving** among *children ever born* (637-2), *reporting of sibling deaths*, **orphanhood status** or **widowhood status**.
ctx_en.en:129: **Probabilities of dying** **(431-1)** or **death probabilities** **(431-1)** are used to study in detail the mortality of a period or of a cohort. They are the probabilities that an individual of exact age *x* will die before exact age x + n, and are represented by the symbol nqx. If n = 1, we talk about **annual death probabilities** **(431-2)**; if n = 5, about **quinquennial death probabilities** **(431-3)**. The **instantaneous death rate** **(431-4)**, or as it is occasionally called the **force of mortality** **(431-4)**, is the limit of the nqx value as *n* tends to zero. The **projective mortality probability** **(431-5)** is the probability that individuals of the same cohort or group of cohorts died between two January 1st)**. The name of this probability comes from its use in the calculation of population projections. It is also equal to 1-Lx+n/Lx, where Lx is the person-years lived by the stationary population from exact age x to exact age x+n. The complement to one of the probability of dying from exact age x to exact age x + n is the **probability of survival** **(431-6)** over this interval. In the preparation of population projections, we use **survival ratios** **(431-7)**; they represent the probability that individuals of the same birth cohort or group of cohorts will still be alive n years later. - **431-1** The probability of death between age x and x + n is defined as the ratio of deaths between ages x and x+n to the number of survivors at exact age x. It is not to be confused with the **central death rate**, the ratio of deaths between ages x and x+n to the mean population alive at that age. The central death rate is written nmx . - **431-6** The probability of survival from age x to age x+n is written npx . - **431-7** A **survival ratio** is the complement to one of the projective mortality probability. Individuals in the cohorts do not have the same age and therefore are not at the same risk of dying.
ctx_en.en:130:
The course of mortality throughout the life cycle may be described by a **life table** **(432-1)**. A life table consists of several **life table functions** **(432-2)**, all of which are mathematically related and may be generally derived when the value of one of them is known. The **survivorship function** **(432-3)** shows the number of **survivors** **(432-4)** of a *cohort* (116-2) of births to various *exact ages* (322-7) on the assumption that the cohort is subjected to the rates of mortality shown. The number of births in the original cohort is known as the **radix** **(432-5)** of the life table and the process by which the original cohort is reduced is known as **attrition** **(432-6)**.
 - **432-4**  The number of survivors to exact age x is denoted by l<sub>x</sub> .
 - **432-5**  The radix is usually a power of 10: 10,000 or 100,000 for example.
ctx_en.en:131:
To the survivors function corresponds a **death function** **(433-1)** which is calculated as the differences between the number of *survivors* (432-4) at different ages. It is named the **distribution of life table deaths** **(433-2)** in order to be distinguished from the crude distribution of deaths. Life tables typically include the **expectation of life** **(433-3)** or **life expectancy** **(433-3)** at age x ; this is the mean number of years to be lived by those surviving to exact age x, given the mortality conditions of the table. The **expectation of life at birth** **(433-4)** is a particular case of expectation of life, and represents the **mean length of life** **(433-4)** of individuals who have been subjected since birth to the mortality of the table. The reciprocal of the expectation of life at birth is the **life table death rate** **(433-5)** or **death rate of the stationary population** **(433-5)**.
 - **433-3**  By integrating the *survivorship function* (432-3) between two exact given ages we obtain the **total number of years lived** by the cohort between these ages; the notation for the total number of years lived between age *x* and *x + n* is *<sub>n</sub>L<sub>x</sub>* . This function is often called the **stationary population** in life table column headings. By summing it from a given age x to the end of life, we obtain the total number of years to be lived after attaining age x by those reaching that age; the conventional notation is T <sub>x</sub> .
 - **433-4**  The notation for the expectation of life at age x is e<sub>x</sub>
ctx_en.en:132: The **median length of life** **(434-1)** sometimes called the **probable length of life** **(434-1)** is the age at which half the original cohort of births have died. After infancy the distribution of deaths by age in the life table will usually have a mode and the corresponding age is called the **modal age at death** **(434-2)**, or sometimes the **normal age at death** **(434-2)**. It may be of interest as an indicator of **human longevity** **(434-3)** or the **length of life** **(434-3)** corresponding more closely to the sense in which the term is used in everyday language than either the average (433-4) or the median length of life. The term **life span** **(434-4)** is used to refer to the maximum possible length of human life.
ctx_en.en:133: A **complete life table** **(435-1)** is usually one in which the values of the *life table functions* (432-2) are given in single years of age. An **abridged life table** **(435-2)** is one in which most functions are given only for certain pivotal ages, frequently spaced at five or ten year intervals after infancy; intermediate values for the functions are usually obtained by some form of interpolation (151-7). The term **life table for selected heads** **(435-3)** is used to refer to a life table relating to the experience of a number of specially selected individuals, such as the clients of a life insurance company, in opposition to **general life tables** **(435-4)** which relate the experience of a whole *population* (101-4). Life tables are generally presented on a sex-specific basis although on occasion they are presented for both sexes. A life table which is based only upon the generalization of empirical relationships is called a **model life table** **(435-5)**.
ctx_en.en:134: A **calendar-year life table** **(436-1)** or **period life table** **(436-1)** (cf. 153-2; 432-1) is one in which the mortality rates used relate to a specified time interval and the *cohort* (116-2) is therefore hypothetical. A **generation life table** **(436-2)**, or **cohort life table** **(436-2)** on the other hand, traces the experience of an actual birth cohort and the mortality rates contained in the table are then spread over a prolonged period, usually about 100 years. A **mortality surface** **(436-3)** is drawn when *probabilities of dying* (431-1) are plotted against age and time period simultaneously in a three-dimensional diagram.
ctx_en.en:135: The **Lexis diagram** **(437-1)** is commonly used to illustrate the usual method for computing death probabilities and other demographic measures. In this diagram, every individual is represented by a **life line** **(437-2)** which begins at birth and ends in the **point of death** **(437-3)**. A method for the study of mortality at very advanced ages has been called the **method of extinct generations** **(437-4)**, because it uses observed deaths for cohorts which have been completely eliminated by mortality.
ctx_en.en:136:
The study of **nuptiality** **(501-1)** deals with the frequency of **marriages** **(501-2)** i.e. of **unions** **(501-3)** between persons of opposite sexes which involve rights and obligations fixed by law or custom; with the characteristics of persons united in marriage; and with the dissolution of such unions. By extension, it also includes the study of other *conjugal unions* (503-8) where their frequency makes their inclusion necessary. A **marriage** **(501-4)** or **wedding** **(501-4)** is the ceremony, prescribed by law or custom, which establishes such a union between a man and a woman as **spouses** **(501-5)**, i.e. **husband** **(501-6)** and **wife** **(501-7)**. The spouses jointly are called a **married couple** **(501-8)**.
 - **501-4**  **Marriage**, n. - **marry**, v. - **married**, adj. - **marriageable**, adj.: capable of contracting a marriage.
 - **501-6**  A man at, or soon before or after his marriage, is a **bridegroom** (abbreviation: **groom**).
 - **501-7**  A woman at, or soon before or after her marriage, is a **bride**.
ctx_en.en:137:
**Marriage laws** **(502-1)** or **marriage customs** **(502-2)** differ in different societies. A person who is married to only one person at a time is called **monogamous** **(502-3)**. A person who is married to several persons simultaneously is called **polygamous** **(502-4)**. A distinction is made between **polyandrous** **(502-5)** societies, where a woman may have several husbands, and **polygynous** **(502-6)** societies, where a man may have several wives. The term "polygamy" is frequently used in the sense of polygyny.
 - **502-3**  **Monogamous**, adj. - **monogamy**, n.
 - **502-4**  **Polygamous**, adj. - **polygamy**, n.
 - **502-5**  **Polyandrous**, adj. - **polyandry**, n.
 - **502-6**  **Polygynous**, adj. - **polygyny**, n.
ctx_en.en:138:
In some countries a legal union can be established only through a **civil marriage** **(503-1)** performed by an official of the state; in other countries a **religious marriage** **(503-2)** in accordance with the regulations of a church is recognized as having legal force. Social or legal recognition may be given under various conditions in different countries to stable unions which have not been solemnized by a legal or religious ceremony, for instance to **customary marriages** **(503-3)** or to **common law marriages** **(503-3)** conforming to local traditions. Different types of relationships and degrees of social acceptance are implied in terms applied to various unions but their significance varies widely in different countries. The term **consensual union** **(503-4)** implies a socially recognized stable union, the term **companionate marriage** **(503-4)** has a similar connotation. The terms **free union** **(503-5)** and **temporary union** **(503-6)** both imply a less stable union that may or may not include **cohabitation** **(503-7)**. Two persons of opposite sexes living in a stable union, whether legal or not, are called a **couple** **(503-8)**. The term **conjugal union** **(503-8)** has been used by demographers to include both legal unions and more or less stable illegal unions.
 - **503-3**  **Concubinage**, n.: a type of illegal union. A concubine in the restricted sense is a woman with an accepted conjugal status inferior to that of a legally recognized wife, particularly in polygynous societies. In other societies, the word concubine is sometimes used loosely to denote any woman other than a wife living in conjugal union with a man. Today such terms as **companion** or **mate** are preferred.
 - **503-7**  **Cohabitation**, n.- **cohabit**, v.
ctx_en.en:139: In many countries a **minimum age at marriage** **(504-1)** is laid down by law. The age differs from country to country and may be different for the two sexes. Marriages among persons closely related by blood are called **consanguineous marriages** **(504-2)** and are generally prohibited by either law or custom. Persons who are forbidden to marry one another for these reasons are said to be within the prohibited **degrees of consanguinity** **(504-3)**.
ctx_en.en:140:
In some countries the **publication of banns** **(505-1)** or **intent to marry** **(505-1)** is a necessary preliminary to a *marriage* (501-4), giving public notice to persons interested, who may then oppose the marriage if they have reason to do so. In many countries a **marriage license** **(505-2)** must be obtained before the marriage ceremony can take place. A **marriage certificate** **(505-3)** is usually delivered to the **newly married couple** **(505-4)** after the ceremony. The **consummation of marriage** **(505-5)** has occurred, or a marriage has been **consummated** **(505-5)** when sexual relations have taken place between the spouses.
 - **505-1**  Before the celebration of the marriage the future spouses are said to be **engaged** or **betrothed**, words which come from the custom of **engagement** or **betrothal** which consists of a more or less formal exchange of promise to marry.
ctx_en.en:141:
**Endogamy** **(506-1)** exists where both spouses must belong to the same group (e.g. tribe, clan). The term is also used to denote a tendency for spouses to be members of the same social or geographical group or **isolate** **(506-2)**, which is generally of limited size. The opposite requirement or tendency is called **exogamy** **(506-3)**. **Mixed marriages** **(506-4)** are marriages between persons of different nationalities, races, religions, etc. When marriage is contracted between persons with certain common characteristics, social, physical or mental, it is called **homogamy** **(506-5)**, the opposite is called **heterogamy** **(506-6)**.
 - **506-1**  **Endogamy**, n. - **endogamous**, adj. 
 - **506-3**  **Exogamy**, n. - **exogamous**, adj.
 - **506-5**  **Homogamy**, n. - **homogamous**, adj.
 - **506-6**  **Heterogamy**, n. - **heterogamous**, adj.
ctx_en.en:142: At the close of **married life** **(510-1)** or **conjugal life** **(510-1)**, the **end of union** **(510-2)** coincides with the **dissolution of marriage** **(510-3)**, i.e. the breaking of all legal obligations resulting from the status of spouse, including the removal of legal obstacles to a new marriage. If a marriage is dissolved by death the surviving spouse is called a **widower** **(510-4)** if male and a **widow** **(510-5)** if female. **Widowed persons** **(510-6)** live in a state of **widowhood** **(510-7)**.
ctx_en.en:143:
Where **divorce** **(511-1)** as an institution is recognized, the dissolution of *marriage* (510-2) may take place through the granting of a **decree of divorce** **(511-2)** to one of the spouses. In some countries a spouse may be **repudiated** **(511-3)** by the other. Persons whose marriages have been dissolved by divorce are called **divorced persons** **(511-4)**. The French words **divorcée** **(511-6)** (woman) or **divorcé** **(511-5)** (man) are sometimes used in English, though the masculine form is rare.
 - **511-1**  **Divorce**, n. and v.
ctx_en.en:144: In some countries the principle of the **indissolubility of marriage** **(512-1)** is upheld by law or custom and *divorce* (511-1) is not allowed; only the death of one of the *spouses* (501-5) may bring about *dissolution of the marriage* (510-3). Under any legal system, however, lack of harmony may lead to **separation** **(512-2)** of the spouses. This may take the form of a **de facto separation** **(512-3)**, either through common consent or as the result of the **desertion** **(512-4)** of one of the spouses by the other. Or it may take the form of a **legal separation** **(512-5)** or **judicial separation** **(512-5)**. A judicial separation absolves the parties from certain obligations, including the duty of living together, or cohabitation, but does not enable either of them to contract a new marriage. Persons whose marriages have been broken by separation are called **separated persons** **(512-6)**. Marriages in which the spouses no longer cohabit but which have not been legally dissolved may be called **broken marriages** **(512-7)**.
ctx_en.en:145: A **decree of nullity** **(513-1)** or an **annulment of marriage** **(513-1)** is a declaration by a court of law that, although a marriage ceremony has taken place, there has been no **valid marriage** **(513-2)**. The expression **dissolved marriage** **(513-3)** is frequently understood to include cases of annulments and of legal separation, although legally the marriage is not dissolved. The term *end of union* (510-2) is more appropriate than dissolution in such cases and may also refer to unions other than marriage.
ctx_en.en:146:
From a legal point of view, any person who meets the conditions set by law or custom to contract a marriage is **marriageable** **(514-1)**, and the **marriageable population** **(514-2)** is made up of such persons; the **non-marriageable population** **(514-3)** consists of those who are not free to do so by law or custom. The **marriage market** **(514-4)**, the **marriageable circle** **(514-5)** or **group of persons** **(514-5)** among whom **mate selection** **(514-6)** takes place however, does not include all marriageable persons; **candidates to marriage** **(514-7)** include only those who are not excluded, at least temporarily, by reasons of health or other circumstances from the marriage market. Widowed or divorced persons may contract a new marriage; there is thus a distinction between a **first marriage** **(514-8)** and a marriage of higher order, or **remarriage** **(514-9)**. Because the **order of marriage** **(514-10)** may differ for the two spouses, the term “first marriage” is ambiguous unless specified as referring to *groom* (501-6*) or to *bride* (501-7*) or to both parties; unless otherwise specified, it refers to a marriage between a bachelor (515-3) and a spinster (515-4).
 - **514-9**  **Remarriage**, n. - **remarry**, v. - **remarried**, adj.
ctx_en.en:147:
The population may be divided into different groups by **conjugal status** **(515-1)**, **marital status** **(515-1)** or **marital condition** **(515-1)**. **Single** **(515-2)** persons, **bachelors** **(515-3)** (men) and **spinsters** **(515-4)** (women), are those who have never been married; they are also sometimes called the **never-married** **(515-2)** class. The class of **married persons** **(515-5)**, **married men** **(515-6)** and **married women** **(515-7)**, consists of those who have been married and whose marriages have not been *dissolved* (513-3). All persons except single persons are **ever-married persons** **(515-8)**.
 - **515-2**  A synonym is **celibate**, adj. - **celibacy**, n.: the state of being single.
ctx_en.en:148:
Relative marriage frequency is measured by **marriage rates** **(520-1)** or **nuptiality rates** **(520-1)**, among which the **crude marriage rate** **(520-2)** gives the ratio of the total number of marriages to the total population in a given period. **Male nuptiality** **(520-3)** and **female nuptiality** **(520-4)** are often different, and can be studied separately. The terms male nuptiality and female nuptiality are used for the marriage frequency of the different sexes. A **sex-specific marriage rate** **(520-5)** can be computed with the appropriate population of each sex as a base. It is usual to distinguish between a **first marriage rate** **(520-6)**, which relates the number of *bachelors* or *spinsters* (515-3 and 4) marrying to the total number of bachelors and spinsters respectively and a **remarriage rate** **(520-7)** which relates the number of remarriages to the total number of widowed and divorced persons. Similar rates can be computed by age or age-group of husband and wife whenever marriages are classified by **age at marriage** **(520-8)** of each spouse; such rates are called **age-specific marriage rates** **(520-9)**. The tabulation of spouses by age at marriage permits the computation of the **mean age at marriage** **(520-10)** or **average age at marriage** **(520-10)** for the given year or period. **Age differences between spouses** **(520-11)** can be analyzed from a classification of the **combined ages** **(520-12)** of the spouses.
 - **520-2**  Sometimes the crude marriage rate is obtained by relating the number of newly married persons to the total population.
 - **520-9**  The terms **marriage frequencies** and **first marriage frequencies** have sometimes been used to refer to the ratio of the number of marriages or first marriages at a certain age, to the total number of persons of that age, irrespective of their marital status. **Cumulated marriage frequencies** and **cumulated first marriage frequencies** are used in cohort studies.
ctx_en.en:149: The prevalence of marriage in a generation of men or women is measured by the **proportion never married** **(521-1)**. This is usually equivalent to the **proportion remaining single** **(521-2)** at an age such as 50 after which first marriages are rare. The proportion remaining single at each age in a cohort can be computed from **first marriage probabilities** **(521-3)**, i.e. the proportion of single persons at exact age x who will marry before exact age x + 1, assuming that there is no mortality. For practical purposes, however, the proportion remaining single is usually obtained from census data as the **proportion single** **(521-4)** at that age in the corresponding cohort. When a classification of first marriages by age of the spouses is available the **mean age at first marriage** **(521-5)**, the **median age at first marriage** **(521-6)** and the **modal age at first marriage** **(521-7)** can all be computed. In the absence of data on the timing of marriages, it is often possible to compute a **singulate mean age at marriage** **(521-8)** from census data on the proportions single by age.
ctx_en.en:150: **Nuptiality tables** **(522-1)** resemble life tables, and combine various nuptiality functions. The **gross nuptiality table** **(522-1)** includes, by age, the *first marriage probabilities* (521-3) and *proportions remaining single* (521-2), as well as the **number of first marriages** **(522-2)** in a cohort of given size subjected to the prevailing nuptiality on the assumption that there is no mortality; it also gives the **numbers remaining single** **(522-3)** at various ages. The **net nuptiality table** **(522-4)** takes mortality as well as nuptiality into account, and is a particular case of *double decrement tables* (153-4). Such a table includes the **single survivors** **(522-5)**, the **ever-married survivors** **(522-6)**, the **probability of single survival** **(522-7)** and the **expectation of unmarried life** **(522-8)**.
ctx_en.en:151:
A **divorce rate** **(523-1)** can be calculated in different ways. The **crude divorce rate** **(523-2)** gives the ratio of the number of divorces to the average population during a given period. The ratio of divorces to the number of married couples is sometimes computed and may be called the **divorce rate for married persons** **(523-3)**. If divorces are tabulated by the age of the divorced person or by duration of marriage, **age-specific divorce rates** **(523-4)** and **duration-specific divorce rates** **(523-5)** can be computed. Another index of divorce frequency is obtained by computing the **number of divorces per new marriage** **(523-6)**.
 - **523-6**  This is a period measure which relates the divorces of one year, either to the marriages of that year, or to a weighted average of the marriages of several years. In cohort analysis, it is possible to relate divorces in successive years to an initial marriage cohort to compute the **cumulated proportion divorced**.
ctx_en.en:152: When the requisite basic statistics are available, **marriage dissolution probabilities** **(524-1)** may be computed, showing for each sex the probability of the marriage being dissolved by death or divorce according to **duration of marriage** **(524-2)**; marriage dissolution tables are an application of double decrement life tables. Remarriage tables for widowed and divorced persons can also be computed, but the most common indices of remarriage are the **relative frequency of remarriage** **(524-3)**, i.e. the proportion of widowed or divorced persons who remarry, often given by age at widowhood or divorce, and by the interval between widowhood or divorce and remarriage. The latter information enables one to compute the **mean interval between widowhood and remarriage** **(524-4)** and the **mean interval between divorce and remarriage** **(524-5)**.
ctx_en.en:153: A person who is never married, widowed, or divorced.
ctx_en.en:154: A woman who is never married, widowed, or divorced.
ctx_en.en:155:
Demographic studies of **fertility** **(601-1)** deal with certain phenomena connected with human **childbearing** **(601-2)** or **reproduction** **(601-2)**. The term **natality** **(601-1)** is sometimes used instead of fertility. These terms refer to the frequency of occurrence of **births** **(601-3)** or more specifically **live births** **(601-4)** — within populations and sub-populations. A birth is the process of delivering a child. Live births or the births of **live-born children** **(601-5)** are distinguished from *late foetal deaths* (cf. 411-5) by evidence of life, such as respiration, movement of voluntary muscles or heartbeat of the child after complete expulsion or extraction. The term **effective fertility** **(601-6)**, which was once used to indicate that late foetal deaths were not counted among the total number of births, should refer to the cases in which the deaths of infants or children are excluded from consideration. The term **total fertility** **(601-7)** has on occasions been used to refer to live births and late foetal deaths combined. The term **differential fertility** **(601-8)** designates fertility differences between the subgroups of a population.
 - **601-1**  On the meaning of the term **fertility** in demography, see also § 623.
 - **601-2**  **Reproduction**, n. - **reproduce**, v. - **reproductive**, adj. Frequently, reproduction refers to the balance of births and deaths (as in § 711) rather than to the process of childbearing or **procreation**.
 - **601-3**  The word **birth** is now commonly used to mean live birth.
 - **601-4**  **Live-born**, adj. also used as noun to mean: infant born alive.
ctx_en.en:156:
**Conception** **(602-1)** results from the **fertilization** **(602-2)** of an **ovum** **(602-3)** by a **spermatozoon** **(602-4)** or **sperm cell** **(602-4)** and marks the beginning of **pregnancy** **(602-5)** or **gestation** **(602-5)** for the impregnated woman. In the course of its development the **product of conception** **(602-6)** is successively called an **embryo** **(602-7)** and then a **foetus** **(602-7)** — sometimes written as **fetus** **(602-7)**. The moment at which the embryo becomes a foetus is not precisely determined: certain scientists set it at the end of 12 weeks or three months of intra—uterine life, although successive developmental stages after the eighth week are often termed foetal. **Nidation** **(602-8)** refers to the implantation of the egg in the wall of the **uterus** **(602-9)** or **womb** **(602-9)**, a process which occurs a few days after fertilization. - **602-1** **Conception**, n.- **conceive**, v. - **602-2** **Fertilization**, n. - **fertilize**, v.
**Artificial fertilization**: fertilization obtained by **artificial insemination**, i.e. by a process other than *coitus* (627-2). - **602-3** A fertilized ovum is called an **egg** or **zygote**. - **602-5** **Pregnancy**, n. - **pregnant**, adj.: gravid, expectant. Certain scientists consider that a pregnancy begins only at the time of *nidation* (602-8) of the egg. - **602-7** **Embryo**, n. - **embryonic**, adj. - **embryology**, n.: the science dealing with the development of the embryo.
**Foetus** or **fetus**, n. - **foetal** or **fetal**, adj. (cf. *411*). - **602-9** **Uterus**, n. - **uterine**, adj.
ctx_en.en:157:
A foetus is said to be **non-viable** **(603-2)** during the first part of a pregnancy and **viable** **(603-1)** thereafter. The change occurs when the foetus becomes capable of independent existence outside its mother, which is commonly considered to take place when the **period of gestation** **(603-3)** or **duration of pregnancy** **(603-3)** has exceeded 28 weeks. If the pregnancy has lasted longer than this, the expulsion of the foetus (alive or dead) takes place during **confinement** **(603-4)**; an earlier explusion associated with an early foetal death is called an **abortion** **(603-5)** (cf. § *604)*. The period of about six weeks after delivery (during which the uterus usually regains its normal size and in which the probability of conception is low) is called the **puerperium** **(603-6)**.
 - **603-1**  **Viable**, adj. - **viability**, n.
 - **603-2**  The minimum period determining viability varies between 20 and 28 weeks among countries, but the World Health Organization has recommended that 28 weeks be the standard time period. Generally the duration of pregnancy is computed from the onset of the **last menses**. This constitutes the **conventional duration of pregnancy**, as opposed to the **true duration of pregnancy**, computed from the time of conception.
 - **603-4**  The actual process of expulsion of the foetus is called **delivery** or **parturition**, which is the termination of **labor**. In addition to those, **confinement** includes expulsion or removal of the **placenta** or **afterbirth**.
 - **603-5**  **Abortion**, n. - **abort**, v.t. or v.i. - **abortifacient**, adj. used as n.: capable of inducing abortion. - **abortionist**, n.: a person who performs abortions. In everyday language, the term *abortion* often takes the meaning of *induced abortion* (604-2), as opposed to *spontaneous abortion* (604-1).
 - **603-6**  **Puerperium**, n. - **puerperal**, adj. (cf. 424-4).
ctx_en.en:158:
Abortions following a non-induced infra-uterine death, which may have occurred some time before expulsion, are called **spontaneous abortions** **(604-1)** or **miscarriages** **(604-1)**, in contrast to **intentional abortions** **(604-2)**, or **induced abortions** **(604-2)**. A **therapeutic abortion** **(604-3)** is one undertaken for medical reasons. The laws of certain countries permit abortions for health or other reasons; these are **legal abortions** **(604-4)**. Abortions which are induced contrary to law are called **illegal abortions** **(604-5)** or **criminal abortions** **(604-5)**. According to the technique used, there are **abortions by curettage** **(604-6)**, **abortions by vacuum aspiration** **(604-7)**, **abortions by dilatation and evacuation** **(604-7)**, **hysterotomies** **(604-8)** (involving surgical cutting into the uterus), and **abortions by medical induction procedures** **(604-9)**.
 - **604-6**  Also called **abortions by dilatation and curettage**, (abbreviated to D and C).
 - **604-7**  Also called **abortions by suction**. When the procedure is used very soon after a presumed conception, the terms **menstrual regulation** or **menstrual extraction** are used.
 - **604-9**  Such procedures involve **amniotic fluid exchange** as in the instance of an **abortion by saline injection**, or the use of **prostaglandins**.
ctx_en.en:159: **Full term deliveries** **(605-1)** occur when the pregnancy has lasted at least 37 weeks, measured in *conventional duration of pregnancy* (603-3*). A pregnancy ending before the normal period is termed a **premature delivery** **(605-2)** or **premature confinement** **(605-2)** or **premature birth** **(605-2)** and the product of this delivery is called a **premature baby** **(605-4)**. Births which are not premature are called **births at term** **(605-3)** or **full-term births** **(605-3)**. The word **prematurity** **(605-5)** is used to refer to phenomena connected with premature delivery. A classification of births by stage of development that does not depend upon an estimate of the period of gestation is used in many countries. In this classification a live-born infant with a **birth weight** **(605-6)** of 2,500 grams (5 1/2 lbs.) or less is said to be **immature** **(605-8)**. **Immaturity** **(605-7)** is often combined with **debility** **(605-9)**, an abnormal state of weakness.
ctx_en.en:160:
At most confinements there is a **single birth** **(606-1)** or **single delivery** **(606-1)** but at some there are **plural births** **(606-2)**, **multiple births** **(606-2)** or **multiple deliveries** **(606-2)**. Two children born during the same confinement are called **twins** **(606-3)** and we may distinguish between **monozygotic twins** **(606-4)**, **uniovular twins** **(606-4)** or **identical twins** **(606-4)** on the one hand, and **dizygotic twins** **(606-5)** or **biovular twins** **(606-5)** on the other. Monozygotic multiple births occur when one ovum splits after fertilization; the resulting children must always be of the same sex. Dizygotic multiple births are due to the simultaneous fertilization of two or more ova and the resulting children may be of different sexes.
 - **606-2**  In British official terminology the term **maternity** is used to denote a confinement resulting in the birth of one or more children; the number of **births per maternity** may be computed.
 - **606-3**  Where a multiple birth results in three children, these are-called **triplets**, four are **quadruplets**, and five **quintuplets**. The terms "twins", "triplets", etc. are generally used in accordance with the total number of deliveries during a confinement; occasionally, however, multiple births are classified only in accordance with the number of children born alive.
ctx_en.en:161:
Births are classified by **legitimacy** **(610-1)**. Strictly speaking, a **legitimate child** **(610-2)** may be defined as one whose father and mother were married to one another at the time of conception. But in practice, the classification depends upon the marital status of the mother at the time of the birth or, after the *dissolution of marriage* (510-3), at the time of conception. A **legitimate birth** **(610-3)** is the delivery of such a .child; other births are **illegitimate births** **(610-4)**. It is general practice to consider as legitimate the children who result from **pre-marital conceptions** **(610-5)** or **pre-nuptial conceptions** **(610-5)** (i.e., conceptions occurring before marriage) provided that the parents are married to each other at the time of the birth. An **illegitimate child** **(610-6)** or **child born out of wedlock** **(610-6)** may be **legitimized** **(610-8)** or **legitimated** **(610-8)** by the subsequent marriage of its parents. The process of **legitimation** **(610-9)**, which varies in different countries, may confer on the illegitimate child some or all of the legal rights of legitimate children. In some legal systems it is possible for a father to grant **recognition** **(610-7)** to, or **acknowledge** **(610-7)**, his illegitimate child, i.e., to admit in legal form that he is the child’s father.
 - **610-1**  In the United States of America, we refer to marital and non-marital births.
 - **610-5**  **Bridal pregnancies** is also used in this connection.
 - **610-6**  The legal term **bastard** has acquired a derogatory meaning but is occasionally used by historical demographers. According to the law of some countries a child is illegitimate if it results from **adulterous relations** or **extra-marital relations** i.e., a connection between a married woman and a man other than her husband, but such a birth is not always registered as illegitimate.
ctx_en.en:162:
Births are also classified by **birth order** **(611-1)**, e.g. first births, second births, etc. Birth order is usually determined by considering all **previous births to the mother** **(611-3)**, and sometimes only **births of the present marriage** **(611-2)**. Birth order is generally based on live births only, but occasionally late foetal deaths are taken into account as well. A classification of women by **confinement order** **(611-4)** is made in the same way as for births by counting all pregnancies which lasted at least 28 weeks, and reckoning multiple births as one confinement (cf. 603-4). Similarly a classification by **pregnancy order** **(611-5)** is made by counting all known pregnancies.
