In medical parlance, a woman is called **nulligravida** **(611-6)** if she has never been pregnant; the terms **primigravida** **(611-7)** and **multigravida** **(611-8)** respectively are used for a woman who is pregnant for the first time or who has been pregnant before. Women are also classified by **parity** **(611-9)**, usually on the basis of the number of children born alive, although in biological literature the term refers to the number of confinements, and a woman who has had no confinement at all is said to be a **nullipara** **(611-10)** or **nulliparous** **(611-10)**. Similarly, a woman is termed a **primipara** **(611-11)** and deemed to be **primiparous** **(611-11)** at her first confinement and a **multipara** **(611-12)** or **multiparous** **(611-12)** at subsequent confinements.
 - **611-1**  **Higher order births** are births occurring after the last specified order, e.g. fifth and higher order births.
 - **611-9**  A woman who has not borne any live children is called a **zero-parity woman**, a **one-parity woman** has borne one child but no more, and so on.
ctx_en.en:163:
Studies of **birth timing** **(612-1)** deal with the length of **birth intervals** **(612-2)**. These include the **interval between marriage and the first birth** **(612-3)** and **intervals between successive births** **(612-4)**. The interval between a birth and a fixed date, such as that of a *census* (202-1 *) or *survey* (203-4), is called an **open birth interval** **(612-5)**; intervals that begin before and end after that date are called **straddling intervals** **(612-6)**. The **interval between marriage and the N<sup>th)** birth** **(612-7)** is also used to study the timing of births.
 - **612-1**  **Birth spacing**, although sometimes found in the sense of birth timing as above, is commonly used to refer to the deliberate efforts of couples to postpone a birth.
 - **612-3**  Also called **first birth intervals**. The **second birth interval** is that between the first and the second birth; and so on.
 - **612-4**  As seen from the vantage of that census or survey, the intervals between the recorded successive births are called **closed birth intervals**.
ctx_en.en:164: In computing the period of **exposure to the risk of conception** **(613-1)** it is necessary to consider **pregnancy intervals** **(613-2)**. The interval between marriage and the first pregnancy is the **conception delay** **(613-3)** or **first pregnancy interval** **(613-3)**. The period between the end of one pregnancy and the beginning of the next is the **inter-pregnancy interval** **(613-4)**. If the time when the woman had no sexual activity is subtracted, a **net inter-pregnancy interval** **(613-5)** is obtained. The period between the end of the last pregnancy and the date of a survey is called an **open inter-pregnancy interval** **(613-6)**.
ctx_en.en:165:
The **reproductive period** **(620-1)** (or in women the **childbearing period** **(620-1)**) begins at **puberty** **(620-2)**. **Menstruation** **(620-3)** — the appearance of the **periods** **(620-4)** or **menses** **(620-4)** in women — also begins at puberty. The first period is called the **menarche** **(620-5)** and menstruation ceases with the **menopause** **(620-6)**, which is also sometimes called the **climacteric** **(620-6)**. In practice, the reproductive period is often made to start, by convention, at 15 years or at the *minimum age at marriage* (504-1) and, for some, to end at 45 or 50 year. The temporary absence of menstruation, be it normal or pathological, is called **amenorrhea** **(620-7)**. **Pregnancy amenorrhea** **(620-8)** occurs after a conception, and **post-partum amenorrhea** **(620-9)** after a confinement.
 - **620-1**  The terms **reproductive ages** or **fecund ages** are also used. 
 - **620-3**  **Menstruation**, n. - **menstruate**, v. - **menstrual**, adj.
 - **620-6**  **Menopause**, n. - **menopausal**, adj. The expression **change of life** is used as a synonym for menopause in colloquial language.
ctx_en.en:166:
The capacity of a man, a woman or a couple to produce a live child is called **fecundity** **(621-1)**. The lack of that capacity is called **infecundity** **(621-2)** or **sterility** **(621-2)**; **inability to conceive** **(621-3)** and **inability to procreate** **(621-10)** are the main, but not the single causes of sterility. Used alone, sterility usually carries the connotation of irreversibility, but occasionally **temporary inability to conceive** **(621-4)** and **temporary sterility** **(621-5)** are distinguished from **permanent inability to conceive** **(621-6)** and **permanent sterility** **(621-7)**. Among women we distinguish **primary sterility** **(621-8)** where the woman has never been able to give birth, and **secondary sterility** **(621-9)**, which arises after one or more children have been born.
 - **621-1**  **Fecundity**, n. - **fecund**, adj. An alternative meaning of the term implies the ability to conceive, rather than to produce a live child. The terms **sub-fecundity** and **sub-fecund** mean either that the capacity to produce a live child is below normal, or that the probability of conception is low.
 - **621-2**  **Sterility**, n. - **sterile**, adj. **Infecundity**, n. - **infecund**, adj.
ctx_en.en:167:
The term *temporary sterility* (621-5) is used even in instances where a woman’s inability to conceive is not the result of a pathological condition.Women are said to have **sterile periods** **(622-1)** in each **menstrual cycle** **(622-2)**, because generally conception can occur only during a few days around the time of **ovulation** **(622-3)**. The period of sterility that extends from *conception* (602-1) to the return of ovulation after a delivery, which includes *pregnancy* (602-5) and is influenced by the duration of **breastfeeding** **(622-4)**, is called the **nonsusceptible period** **(622-5)**, particularly in mathematical models of reproduction. Temporary sterility is also used to refer to the occurrence of **anovulatory cycles** **(622-6)** (i.e., menstrual cycles in which ovulation does not occur) or to abnormal periods of amenorrhea. The **sub-fecundity** **(622-7)** of very young women is commonly called **adolescent sterility** **(622-8)**; it would be better to talk about **adolescent sub-fecundity** **(622-8)**.
 - **622-5**  The period between delivery and the return of ovulation is often called the period of **post-partum sterility**.
 - **622-6**  Also called anovular cycles.
ctx_en.en:168:
**Fertility** **(623-1)** and **infertility** **(623-2)** refer to reproductive performance rather than capacity, and are used according to whether there was actual childbearing or not during the period under review. When it concerns the complete reproductive period, the term **total infertility** **(623-3)** may be used while **permanent infertility** **(623-4)** may extend from a certain age or marriage duration to the end of the childbearing years. **Voluntary infertility** **(623-5)** is used when the absence of procreation corresponds to a decision of the couple (503-8).It should be noted that in many Latin languages, the cognates of fertility and fecundity are used in a sense diametrically opposite to that in English. Thus, the French *fécondité* and the Spanish *fecundidad* are properly translated by fertility, and *fertilité* and *fertilidad* by fecundity. - **623-1** **Fertility**, n. - fertile, adj. - **623-2** **Infertility**, n. - infertile, adj.
**Childlessness**, n. - **childless**, adj. : refer to the state of a women, man or couple who have been so far infertile.
ctx_en.en:169:
The *fertility* (623-1) of couples will depend upon their **reproductive behavior** **(624-1)**. A distinction is drawn between **planners** **(624-2)**, couples who attempt to regulate the number and *spacing* (612-1*) of their births, and **non-planners** **(624-3)**, couples who make no such attempt. **Family planning** **(624-4)** has a broader meaning than **family limitation** **(624-4)** which refers to efforts not to exceed the **number of children wanted** **(624-5)**. The terms **birth control** **(624-6)** or **fertility regulation** **(624-6)** are not restricted to the activities of married persons.
 - **624-4**  A classification according to **family planning status** distinguishes couples who have not tried to regulate the number and spacing of their children from those who have tried to do so.
 - **624-5**  **Unwanted births** or **unintended births** are distinguished from **unplanned births** that may have occurred at a time that was not intended, and perhaps outside of wedlock.
ctx_en.en:170:
Family planning implies a concern with **planned parenthood** **(625-1)** or **responsible parenthood** **(625-1)**, i.e., the desire to determine the number and spacing of births in conformity with the best interest of each couple, or of society. The number of children expected by a couple may differ from the **desired number of children** **(625-2)** and/or **intended number of children** **(625-2)** reported by the couple in a survey. Even if these goals are not revised, they may be exceeded as a result of **contraceptive failures** **(625-3)** ; the frequency of the latter depends on **contraceptive effectiveness** **(625-4)** which has two aspects. **Theoretical effectiveness** **(625-5)** or **physiological effectiveness** **(625-5)** indicates how reliable a method is when used all the time according to directions. **Use effectiveness** **(625-6)** measures its reliability when used in everyday situations by a given population. Reasoning in terms of *residual fecundability* (638-7), use effectiveness is usually measured by the **contraceptive failure rate** **(625-7)** which relates the number of unintended conceptions to the length of exposure to the risk of conceiving.
 - **625-2**  In other terms, **birth expectations** differ from **reproductive intentions**. A distinction is made between **desired family size**, the number of children a woman, man or couple wants to have, and the **ideal family size** which they envision for their society. **Intended family size** may be lower than desired family size.
 - **625-3**  **Unplanned births** are often opposed to **planned births**.
 - **625-4**  Not to be confused with the **demographic effectiveness** of a family planning program (see 626-7), or of a method in a population.
 - **625-4**  5. and 6. **Efficacy** is a synonym for effectiveness in these expressions.
ctx_en.en:171:
A **family planning program** **(626-1)** seeks to introduce and diffuse birth control in a group of **potential users** **(626-2)** or in a **target population** **(626-2)**. Teams of **fieldworkers** **(626-3)**, including **canvassers** **(626-3)**, **motivators** **(626-3)** and **distributors** **(626-3)**, attempt to reach and convince the population to use contraception or abortion. The success of the program can be measured by the **proportion of new acceptors** **(626-4)** in the target population, or by the **acceptance rate** **(626-4)**; for the acceptors of contraception, the **continuation rate** **(626-5)** after a certain lapse of time and its complement, the **termination rate** **(626-6)** or **drop-out rate** **(626-6)** are also computed. Estimates of the numbers and proportions of **births averted** **(626-7)** reflect the *demographic effectiveness* (625-4*) of the program. Contraceptive prevalence in a population is estimated by the **proportion of current users** **(626-8)** of contraception from a relevant universe, such as married women of reproductive age.
 - **626-8**  Special **surveys of knowledge, attitudes and practice** of contraception have been called **KAP surveys** in abbreviation.
ctx_en.en:172:
**Contraception** **(627-1)** refers to measures which are taken in order to prevent **sexual intercourse** **(627-2)** or **coitus** **(627-2)** from resulting in conception; the term covers contraceptive *sterilization* (631-1). **Birth control methods** **(627-3)** is used in a broader sense than **contraceptive methods** **(627-3)** to include induced *abortion* (604-2). **Abstinence** **(627-4)** from coitus, particularly *periodic abstinence* (628-4) is often included among contraceptive or birth control methods.
 - **627-1**  **Contraception**, n. - **contraceptor**, n.: one who practices contraception. **Contraceptive**, adj. : used for contraception.
 - **627-4**  **Abstinence**, n. - **abstain**, v.
ctx_en.en:173:
A distinction is frequently drawn between **appliance methods** **(628-1)** of contraception and **non-appliance methods** **(628-2)**. One principal non-appliance method of contraception is **coitus interruptus** **(628-3)** or **withdrawal** **(628-3)**. Another non-appliance method of contraception is **periodic abstinence** **(628-4)** or the **rhythm method** **(628-4)**, in which coitus is avoided during the period when the woman is believed to be fecund and takes place only during the so-called **safe period** **(628-5)** of the menstrual cycle. The **basal body temperature method** **(628-6)** refers to the method in which the woman keeps track of her temperature to identify the safe period.
 - **628-1**  Appliance methods include not only **barrier methods** which are used to prevent the union of the sperm and ovum, but also methods using other **contraceptive devices** such as the intra-uterine device (629-10) and other types of **contraceptives** such as the pill (630-4).
 - **628-4**  The term **natural family planning methods** has been applied collectively to cover the rhythm method, the basal body temperature method, and other techniques like cervical mucous method which attempt to identify stages of the woman’s ovulatory cycle.
ctx_en.en:174: The barrier methods which are more commonly used alone or in combination include the **condom** **(629-1)** or **sheath** **(629-1)**, used by men, and the **cervical cap** **(629-2)** or **pessary** **(629-2)**, the **diaphragm** **(629-3)**, **tampon** **(629-4)** or **sponge** **(629-4)**, **contraceptive jelly** **(629-5)**, **suppository** **(629-6)**, **foam tablets** **(629-7)** and **douche** **(629-8)** with or without **spermicide** **(629-9)**, used by women. There are various types of **intra-uterine devices** **(629-10)** (abbreviated to **IUD** **(629-10)**), including the **loop** **(629-10)**, the **coil** **(629-10)**, the **copper T** **(629-10)**, etc.
ctx_en.en:175: **Oral contraceptives** **(630-1)** are a method of **hormonal contraception** **(630-2)** or **contraception by steroids** **(630-3)**. These inhibit ovulation by regular ingestion of the **pill** **(630-4)**, or by injections or implants.
ctx_en.en:176:
**Sterilization** **(631-1)** results from various surgical procedures: on the male, **vasectomy** **(631-2)** or **occlusion** **(631-3)** involves tying and cutting the vas deferens; on the female **tubal ligation** **(631-4)** and **salpingectomy** **(631-5)** or **tubectomy** **(631-5)** involve interventions on the fallopian tubes. **Hysterectomy** **(631-6)** or excision of the uterus, also involves sterilization of the woman.
 - **631-4** and 5. Various procedures are used to gain access to the Fallopian tubes, such as **laparotomy**, **colpotomy** or **laparoscopy**.
ctx_en.en:177:
The general term **birth rate** **(632-1)** refers to a rate calculated by relating the number of live births observed in a population or sub-population during a given period to the size of the population or sub-population during the period. The rate is usually stated per 1,000, and the most usual period is one year. Where the term birth rate is used without qualification, it is understood to be the **crude birth rate** **(632-2)**, and all live births are related to the entire population. The **total birth rate** **(632-3)** based on live births and late foetal deaths is sometimes calculated. **Marital birth rates** **(632-4)** (**legitimate birth rates** **(632-4)**) and **non-marital birth rates** **(632-5)** (**illegitimate birth rates** **(632-5)**) are also calculated with legitimate and illegitimate births in the numerator and the currently married and unmarried female population, respectively, in the denominator. The **illegitimacy ratio** **(632-6)**, the number of illegitimate births per 1,000 total births, is more frequently used, however. To compare the fertility of different populations, **standardized birth rates** **(632-7)** are often used to eliminate the effect on the birth rate of certain differences in structure of the population (most commonly the age and sex structure). The **child-woman ratio** **(632-8)**, most commonly the number of children aged 0 to 4 per 1,000 women of childbearing age, e.g., 15 to 49, is used as an index of fertility when reliable birth statistics are not available.
 - **632-4**  The denominator of the marital and non-marital birth rate is sometimes the total population.
 - **632-5**  See note 4.
ctx_en.en:178:
The term **fertility rate** **(633-1)** is often used when the denominator of the birth rate is restricted to a group of individuals of the same sex in the reproductive ages (620-1). This denominator is commonly the mid-year population in the stated period, but it may also be the number of years lived by the group during the period, or the mean size of the group. Unless otherwise indicated, these rates are **female fertility rates** **(633-2)**, and the rates are calculated for groups of women; the number of years lived by a given number of women in an interval is called the number of **woman years** **(633-3)**. **Male fertility rates** **(633-4)** are computed sometimes in an analogous manner. Fertility rates are generally expressed as births per thousand (implied: individuals of the same category — sex, age, marital status, etc. — cf. 133-4*). **Marital fertility rates** **(633-5)** or **legitimate fertility rates** **(633-5)** relate the total number of legitimate births (610-3) to the number of currently married women; **non-marital fertility rates** **(633-6)** or **illegitimate fertility rates** **(633-6)** relate the total number of illegitimate births (610-4) to the number of single, widowed and divorced women. **Overall fertility rates** **(633-7)** make no distinction according (610-1) to the marital status of the parents. The **general fertility rate** **(633-8)** relates the total number of births to all women of reproductive age regardless of marital status. Rates based on a narrower age range (usually one-year or five-year age groups) are called **age-specific fertility rates** **(633-9)** or **age-specific birth rates** **(633-9)**.
 - **633-1**  In many expressions used in this and following paragraphs, **birth rate** is used synonymously with fertility rate.
 - **633-5**  **Marital fertility** or **legitimate fertility**: the fertility of married persons (see 635-1).
 - **633-6**  **Non-marital fertility** or **illegitimate fertility**: the fertility of unmarried persons.
ctx_en.en:179: **Order-specific fertility rates** **(634-1)** relate births of a certain order to a number of women, to a number of marriages or to a number of births of the preceding order. **Parity-specific fertility rates** **(634-2)** or **parity-specific birth rates** **(634-2)** not only restrict the numerator to births of a given order, but also restrict the denominator to the women of the *parity* (611-6) *at risk* (134-2), e.g., second order births to one-parity women. Such rates are usually age-specific or duration-specific. In **parity-specific birth probabilities** **(634-3)**, the numerator consists of the number of births of order x + 1 occurring during a period, and the denominator consists of the number of women of parity x at the beginning of the same period.
ctx_en.en:180: When studying **marital fertility** **(635-1)** it is possible to arrange the data by *marriage cohorts* (116-2) of the mothers, and **marriage duration-specific fertility rates** **(635-2)** are often computed in preference to **age-specific marital fertility rates** **(635-3)**.
ctx_en.en:181:
The term **cohort fertility** **(636-1)** refers to the reproductive performance of particular birth or marriage cohorts (116-2). When the age-specific or marriage duration-specific fertility rates are summed from the cohort’s beginning of exposure to risk until some later date, we speak of **cumulative fertility** **(636-2)**: ** cumulative age-specific fertility** **(636-3)** or **cumulative duration-specific marital fertility** **(636-3)** when then ending date is that of a womans birthday or marriage (501-4), **completed fertility** **(636-4)** or **lifetime fertility** **(636-4)** is the cumulative fertility until the date when all members of the cohort have reached the end of the reproductive period. The sum of the products of the fertility rates of the cohort by the probability of survival of the women to successive ages could be called the **cumulative net fertility** **(636-5)**, **net cumulative age-specific fertility** **(636-6)** or **net cumulative duration-specific marital fertility** **(636-6)** and **net complete fertility** **(636-7)** or **net lifetime fertility** **(636-7)** of the cohort.
 - **636-4**  Before the end of the reproductive period, the terms incomplete fertility or fertility to date are employed to show that the cohort’s cumulative fertility may be expected to increase.
ctx_en.en:182: Censuses and surveys may provide information on fertility when they include questions on the number of children born to enumerated women or couples, either during the **current marriage** **(637-1)**, or overall. The **mean number of children ever born per woman** **(637-2)** or **average parity** **(637-2)** can be computed. The number of children per couple is sometimes called **average family size** **(637-3)**. It is also possible to calculate the **mean number of births per marriage** **(637-4)**. Special attention is paid to **completed fertility of marriages** **(637-5)**, those in which the wife had reached the end of the reproductive years before the marriage was dissolved. The **final parity** **(637-6)** or **completed parity** **(637-6)**, i.e., the mean number of children per woman past the childbearing age, is not very different from *completed fertility* (636-4). The tabulation of final parity or completed fertility by number of children serves to compute series of **parity progression ratios** **(637-7)**; these are fractions whose denominator is the number of women with *n* children, and whose numerator is the number of women with *n* + 1 children. Special studies yield information on **family formation** **(637-8)** and the **family life cycle** **(637-8)**. Among those, **frequency of premarital conceptions** **(637-9)**, *birth intervals* (612-1) and the **age at the birth of the last child** **(637-10)** for women of completed fertility are of particular interest.
ctx_en.en:183:
**Fertility histories** **(638-1)** or **reproductive histories** **(638-1)** are accounts obtained for individual women of the important events in their reproductive lives, such as marriages, pregnancies, births, infant deaths, etc., and their dates. Fertility histories are often obtained retrospectively from surveys. **Family forms** **(638-1)** are used in *historical demography* (102-1), where they are established for a married couple and its children by **family reconstitution** **(638-2)** on the basis of *vital records* (211-3). A woman’s **pregnancy history** **(638-3)** or **pregnancy record** **(638-3)** contains detailed information about her pregnancies including the date when each began and ended, and the outcome of the pregnancy. Such detailed records on the timing of fertility have been used for various purposes. For example, they can provide information on **natural fertility** **(638-4)**, i.e., fertility in the absence of *family limitation* (624-4). They are also used to estimate **fecundability** **(638-5)**, the probability of conceiving per *menstrual cycle* (622-2). A distinction is made between **natural fecundability** **(638-6)**, in the absence of contraception, and **residual fecundability** **(638-7)** in the opposite instance. The term **effective fecundability** **(638-8)** designates a fecundability that is reckoned in terms of conceptions that result in live births only. The **conception rate** **(638-9)** during the period of *exposure to risk* often estimated using the **Pearl index** **(638-10)** (613-1) is used to measure the effectiveness of contraception during periods of contraceptive use.
 - **638-1**  Birth histories are usually limited to live births.
 - **638-6**  When used alone, the word fecundability stands for natural fecundability.
ctx_en.en:184:
A summary index of **period fertility** **(639-1)**, i.e., the fertility of a particular year or period, computed by the summation of the series of age-specific fertility rates constituting the **fertility schedule** **(639-2)** and representing a **synthetic measure of fertility** **(639-3)**, is the **total fertility rate** **(639-4)** or **total fertility** **(639-4)**. Other summary period indices can be obtained, such as the **total marital fertility rate** **(639-5)**, the summation of marriage duration-specific fertility rates, and the **order-specific total fertility rate** **(639-6)**, the summation of age-specific fertility rates order by order. The **ratio of births to marriages** **(639-7)** is computed by relating the number of births of a given year, either to the marriages of the year, or to a weighted average of the marriages of the current and of the preceding years.
 - **639-2**  Also, **fertility distribution** or **fertility function**.
 - **639-4**  This is not a rate in the meaning of (133-4). Total fertility for a given year represents the number of children that would be bom per 1,000 women if they experienced no mortality and were subject to the age-specific fertility rates observed for that year. The **period gross reproduction rate** (see 711-4) which is derived by multiplying the total fertility rate by the proportion of female births, has often been used in the past, but the total fertility rate is preferred at present as the summary index of period fertility. 
 - **639-5**  Or **total marital fertility**. The term is also used to describe the sum of the age-specific marital fertility rates above age 20.
ctx_en.en:185: Where *induced abortion* (604-2) has been legalized, it is possible to compile statistics on *legal abortions* (604-4). The **abortion rate** **(640-1)** is a measure of the frequency of abortion in a population during a given period, usually a year. Abortions may be related to the total population or to the number of women in the reproductive ages and may be specific for age, parity or any other characteristic. The **abortion ratio** **(640-2)** is a measure of the frequency of abortions in relation to the number of *live births* (601-4) during the same period. The **life-time abortion rate** **(640-3)** is the sum of **age-specific abortion rates** **(640-4)** and is a synthetic measure of abortion per woman or per 1000 women. These rates are the ratio of the number of abortions reported at each age to years lived by all women of the same age. If women can be classified according to their marital status, **abortion rates by age and marital status** **(640-5)** can be obtained. It is often also relevant to divide the number of abortions by the number of conceptions and so to calculate the **probability that a pregnancy results in an abortion by age and marital status** **(640-6)**.
ctx_en.en:186: Number of years lived by a givean number of men in an interval.
ctx_en.en:187: The interaction of fertility, mortality and migration leads to a consideration of **population growth** **(701-1)**. A **zero population growth** **(701-10)** refers to a population of constant size. It is convenient to regard **population decline** **(701-2)** as **negative growth** **(701-3)**. A distinction may be drawn between a **closed population** **(701-4)** in which there is no migration either inwards or outwards and whose growth depends entirely on the difference between births and deaths, and an **open population** **(701-5)** in which there may be migration. The growth of an open population consists of the **balance of migration** **(701-6)** or **net migration** **(701-6)** and **natural increase** **(701-7)**, which is the **excess of births over deaths** **(701-8)** or **deficit of births over deaths** **(701-9)** sometimes called the **balance of births and deaths** **(701-8)**. Any change in one variable affects the overall growth and structure of a population; in this context **growth effects** **(701-11)** and **structural effects** **(701-12)** are determined.
ctx_en.en:188:
The ratio of total growth in a given period to the mean population of that period is called the **growth rate** **(702-1)**. Occasionally this rate is computed with the population at the beginning of the period rather than with the mean population as a denominator. When population increase over a period of more than one calendar year is studied, the **mean annual rate of growth** **(702-2)** may be computed. In computing this rate it is sometimes assumed that the population is subjected to **exponential growth** **(702-3)** during the period, and time is treated as a continuous variable. The size of an **exponential population** **(702-4)** would grow as an exponential function of time. The **exponential growth rate** **(702-5)** is equal to the **instantaneous rate of growth** **(702-5)**. The ratio of natural increase (701-7) to the average population during a period is called the **crude rate of natural increase** **(702-6)** and is equal to the difference between the crude birth rate and the crude death rate. The **vital index** **(702-7)** is the ratio of the number of births to the number of deaths during a period; this measure is no longer much used.
 - **702-3**  When time is treated as a discrete variable, reference is made to **geometric growth**. 
 - **702-4**  This is occasionally called a **Malthusian population**, but the term is ambiguous in view of its sociological connotations (see 906-1).
ctx_en.en:189:
It can be shown that when a *closed population* (701-4) is subjected to constant *age-specific fertility* and *mortality rates* (631-8; 412-1) for a sufficiently long period of time, its annual rate of increase will tend to become constant. This constant rate of increase is called the **intrinsic rate of natural increase** **(703-1)**, and a population which has reached this stage is called a **stable population** **(703-2)**. The proportion of persons in different age groups in such a population will be constant, i.e., the population will have a **stable age distribution** **(703-3)**. This stable age distribution is independent of the **initial age distribution** **(703-4)** and depends only on the fertility and mortality rates that are kept constant. Human populations never reach exact stability in practice, as fertility and mortality rates constantly change, but the computation of a stable population as a model and of its intrinsic rates may provide an index of the **growth potential** **(703-5)** of a set of age-specific fertility rates applied to a non stabilized age structure. Related to the growth potential, the moment of inertia of a population or **demographic momentum** **(703-11)** should be mentioned: it refers to the dynamics hidden in the age structure due to a delayed growth response caused by the biological fact that from the time of birth of a *cohort* (116-2) to the beginning of their period of *fertility* (620-1) a certain amount of time passes. A population may for this reason still grow, even though the birth rate drops long ago. The reverse case is also possible. The momentum is particularly altered in case of discontinuity in the evolution of births and abrupt reversals of trends. A stable population in which the intrinsic rate of natural increase is zero is called a **stationary population** **(703-6)**. In such a population the numbers in a given age group are equal to the integral of the *survivorship function* (431-3) of the life table taken between the upper and lower age limits of the group, multiplied by a factor of proportionality common to all age groups. A **quasi-stable population** **(703-7)** is a formerly stable population with constant fertility and gradually changing mortality; characteristics of this type of population are similar to those of a **semi-stable population** **(703-8)** which is a closed population with a constant age structure. A **logistic population** **(703-9)** is a population growing in accordance with the **logistic law** **(703-10)** of growth, i.e., a population in which the growth rate decreases as a linear function of the population already alive and which will tend asymptotically to an upper limit. - **703-1** The intrinsic rate, also called by its inventor Lotka, the **true rate of natural increase**, is equal to the difference between the **intrinsic birth rate** (or **stable birth rate**) and the **intrinsic death rate** (or **stable death rate**). - **703-2** **Stable**, adj. - **stability**, n. - **stabilize**, v.
**Stable population analysis** uses the properties of stable population models to estimate various characteristics of real populations. - **703-6** **Stationary**, adj. - **stationarity**, n.
ctx_en.en:190:
The theory of **population replacement** **(710-1)** or **population reproduction** **(710-1)** (see § *116*) treats population as a **renewable resource** **(710-2)** in the mathematical sense of the term. A distinction is drawn between **gross reproduction** **(710-3)** or **gross replacement** **(710-3)**, where no account is taken of mortality before the end of the reproductive period (620-1), and **net reproduction** **(710-4)** or **net replacement** **(710-4)**, in which this mortality is taken into account.
 - **710-1**  Also **reproductivity**. For another sense of reproduction see 601-2.
ctx_en.en:191: In this study of replacement a number of indices, **replacement rates** **(711-1)** or **reproduction rates** **(711-1)** are used. Reproduction rates are generally **female reproduction rates** **(711-2)** or **maternal reproduction rates** **(711-2)**. The female **net reproduction rate** **(711-3)** is defined as the average number of live daughters that would be born to a hypothetical female *birth cohort* (116-2) which would be subjected to a set of current *age-specific fertility* (631-8) and *mortality rates* (401-2). A female **gross reproduction rate** **(711-4)** is computed similarly on the assumption that mortality before the end of the reproductive age is zero. **Male reproduction rates** **(711-5)** or **paternal reproduction rates** **(711-5)** can be computed analogously using male births and a male birth cohort, and certain types of **joint reproduction rates** **(711-6)** which take both sexes into account have been proposed. Where the experience of an actual cohort is used in the construction of reproduction rates, **cohort reproduction rates** **(711-7)** or **generation reproduction rates** **(711-7)** are obtained. The mortality and the fertility rates used in the construction of these rates will refer to different periods of time. Where statistics of fertility by age are not available, the so-called **replacement index** **(711-8)** may be used. This ratio relates the quotient of the population of children of a given age (as a rule those 0-4 years) to the number of women of childbearing age in the actual population, to the corresponding quotient in the *stationary population* (703-6).
ctx_en.en:192: Other replacement indices are also computed. For instance, the net reproduction rate is sometimes split into a **legitimate component** **(712-1)** and an **illegitimate component** **(712-2)**. Again, a **nuptial reproduction rate** **(712-3)** has been computed, showing the number of legitimate daughters that will be born to a newly-born female if current rates of mortality, fertility, nuptiality and dissolution of marriage remain unchanged. Generally such rates are for females, but it would be possible to compute analogous rates for males.
ctx_en.en:193:
The *net reproduction rate* (711-3) and the *intrinsic rate of natural increase* (703-1) are closely related to one another. The net reproduction rate measures the increase in the *stable population* (703-2) implied by the given age-specific fertility and mortality rates over a period equivalent to the **mean length of a generation** **(713-1)** or the **mean interval between successive generations** **(713-1)**. This length of a female generation is equal to the **mean age of mothers** **(713-2)** giving birth to live daughters, with current age-specific fertility and mortality rates. Period reproduction rates are current indices (cf. *152*) which relate to **hypothetical cohorts** **(713-3)** or **synthetic cohorts** **(713-3)**.
 - **713-2**  The **mean age of fertility**, i.e., the mean age of the fertility schedule is only approximately equal to the mean length of a generation. The mean length of a male generation similarly is equal to the **mean age of fathers** at the birth of their children.
ctx_en.en:194:
**Population projections** **(720-1)** are calculations which show the future development of a population when certain assumptions are made about the future course of population change, usually with respect to fertility, mortality and migration. They are in general purely formal calculations, developing the implications of the assumptions that are made. A **population forecast** **(720-2)** is a projection in which the assumptions are considered to yield a realistic picture of the probable future development of a population. Although the **projection period** **(720-3)** is variable, **short-term forecasts** **(720-4)** are the rule, as the margin of error to which forecasts are subject increases considerably as the length of the forecast’s period increases. The most frequently used method of projection is the **component method** **(720-5)** or **cohort-component method** **(720-5)** which takes the population distributed by age and sex at a **base date** **(720-6)** and carries it forward in time, cohort by cohort, on the basis of separate allowances for fertility, mortality and migration. When matrix algebra is used for component projections, the method is sometimes called **matrix method of projection** **(720-7)**.
 - **720-1**  Projections are also made in terms of educational, economic and social characteristics. **Backward projections** which might be more accurately called **retrojections**, use similar methods to trace the past evolution of the population.
ctx_en.en:195:
**Estimates of the population** **(721-1)** by size and composition at various dates in the past and present may be made by various methods, including many of the methods used for *population projections* (720-1). **Demographic estimates** **(721-2)** include estimates of the population and of such characteristics as *fertility* (601-1), *mortality* (401-1), etc. The **annual estimates of population** **(721-5)** from the last census is carried out on the basis of the last census and vital statistics in subsequent years. **Intercensal estimates** **(721-3)** relate to dates intermediate to two or more *censuses* (202-1), and take the results of these censuses into account. The **error of closure** **(721-4)** is the difference between the size of a population enumerated at a new census and the population estimated for that census date on the basis of a previous census, the excess of births over deaths, and *net migration* (805-2) during the intercensal period. This difference represents the balance of errors in the data on births, deaths, net migration, and the coverage of the two censuses.
 - **721-3**  **Postcensal estimates** take the results of a previous census into account, but not those of the next census.
ctx_en.en:196:
A **demographic model** **(730-1)** consists of a theoretical construct representing the evolution of a population (of individuals, couples, families, households, etc.) and its structure on the basis of its initial state and the effect of various demographic variables (such as fertility, fecundability, mortality, etc.). In a **static model** **(730-2)**, these variables remain constant; in a **dynamic model** **(730-3)**, they are allowed to change over time. A further distinction is made between **deterministic models** **(730-4)** which assign functional relations between definite values of the variables, as if the studied population were infinitely large, and **stochastic models** **(730-5)** or **probabilistic models** **(730-5)** which consider the probability of various events occurring to individuals over the duration of the process under study. The model may be set out in mathematical formulas or take the form of a **simulation** **(730-6)** where specific values of the variables are included in a system of relations. **Macrosimulations** **(730-7)** may for example involve population projections made by the *component method* (720-5). In **microsimulations** **(730-8)**, events are made to occur randomly to individuals or groups over time according to sets of probabilities assigned to the variables in the model.
 - **730-1**  The word is also used as an adjective in such expressions as **model tables**.
ctx_en.en:197:
The study of **spatial mobility** **(801-1)** or **geographic mobility** **(801-1)** is concerned with the quantitative aspects of **moves** **(801-2)** made by individuals in geographic space. The distinguishing characteristic of **migration** **(801-3)** is that it involves a change in *usual place of residence* (310-6*) and implies movement across an administrative boundary. The administrative unit left by the migrant is the **place of origin** **(801-4)** or **place of departure** **(801-4)**; the unit to which the migrant goes is the **place of destination** **(801-5)** or **place of arrival** **(801-5)**. The concept of migration is often not applied to moves made by persons without a fixed place of residence, for example, *nomads* are excluded from the count of migrants in many countries. In practice it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between migration, which implies a relatively permanent change of residence, and **temporary moves** **(801-6)**, except on the basis of criteria of **length of absence** **(801-7)** from the place of origin or **duration of stay** **(801-8)** at the place of destination. In general, geographic mobility does not include short-term trips which involve no change of usual residence, even though such moves may deserve study because of their economic and social importance. **Commuting** **(801-9)** involves the daily or weekly journey from place of residence to place of work or schooling; **seasonal moves** **(801-10)** have a yearly periodicity. **Transits** **(801-11)**, which are moves across a territory to reach a destination, do not involve migration with respect to the territory crossed. **Tourist traffic** **(801-12)** or **vacationing** **(801-12)** also are not included in geographic mobility.
 - **801-1**  *Spatial mobility* is distinguished from *social mobility* (920-4) and *occupational mobility* (921-3).
 - **801-3**  **Migration**, n. - **migrate**, v. - **migrant**, n.: one who migrates, also used as adj. - **migratory**, adj.: pertaining to migration. The term *migration* refers to a process and cannot serve in English (in contrast to French) to describe a particular *move*; it is rarely used in the plural. Some authors view all *residential mobility* (803-6) as migration. For most, however, migratory moves involve the crossing of a boundary, and the administrative unit selected is called the **migration defining area**. 
 - **801-5**  The terms **country of arrival** and **country of reception** are appropriate when *international migration* is the subject of interest.
 - **801-9**  **Commute**, v. - **commuter**, n.: one who regularly travels from his place of residence to his place of work. The expression **journey to work** is also used to describe this type of movement.
 - **801-10**  **Seasonal movement** is more accurate than the frequently used term **seasonal migration** since these moves rarely involve a change of usual residence.
ctx_en.en:198:
When migration is observed over time, it is convenient to compare the **place of residence at a fixed past date** **(802-1)** or the **place of last previous residence** **(802-2)** with the **place of current residence** **(802-3)**. An individual whose administrative unit of residence differs at the beginning and end of a certain interval is identified as a **migrant** **(802-4)**. Migrants may be classified as **emigrants** **(802-5)** or **out-migrants** **(802-5)** with respect to their place of origin and as **immigrants** **(802-6)** or **in-migrants** **(802-6)** with respect to their place of current residence. When a census or survey has included a question on **previous place of residence** **(802-2)**, the information generated concerns in fact the **latest migration** **(802-7)** or **latest change of residence** **(802-7)**, whatever its date. A migrant is any individual who has had at least one prior residence in a different administrative unit from his or her current residence; such an individual can be considered to have **migrated into** **(802-8)** the current residence, and **migrated out** **(802-9)** of the previous one. A **lifetime migrant** **(802-11)** is a person whose **place of birth** **(802-10)** was in a different administrative unit from his or her current residence. In specific cases, migrants can be qualified as **emigrants for political, religious or ethical reasons** **(802-12)**, or **immigrants for political, religious or ethical reasons** **(802-13)**.
 - **802-4**  Strictly speaking, under this concept a migrant must have been born before the beginning of the **migration defining interval** and must survive until the end. This definition is sometimes extended to include children born during the interval who are allocated to the place of residence of their mother at the beginning of the interval. The number of recorded migrants is not necessarily equal to the number of moves which occurred during the interval for these individuals, as any one may have moved several times in the interval, or even have returned to his previous place of residence by the time of the census or survey.
 - **802-10**  Usually the place of birth is defined as the place of usual residence of the mother at the time of the birth even though custom or the location of medical facilities may have resulted in the birth occurring elsewhere.
ctx_en.en:199:
The population of a *sovereign country* (305-3) may be involved in **internal migration** **(803-1)** when both *place of departure* (801-4) and *place of destination* (801-5) are within the country, or in **international migration** **(803-2)** which occurs across national boundaries. The term **external migration** **(803-3)** is sometimes encountered in the latter sense. International migration is called **immigration** **(803-4)** or **emigration** **(803-5)** according to whether the country in question is the country of destination or the country of origin, respectively. When the country is divided into sub-areas, movement within the boundaries of each sub-area are **local moves** **(803-6)** and constitute **residential mobility** **(803-6)**, while movement between sub-areas is called **in-migration** **(803-7)** or **out-migration** **(803-8)** depending on whether the sub-area considered is the place of destination or the place of origin for the migrants. A **migration stream** **(803-9)** is a group of migrants having a common origin and destination. The larger stream between two sub-areas is called the **dominant stream** **(803-10)** and the smaller the **counterstream** **(803-11)**.
 - **803-1**  The definitions of migration in this paragraph can be extended to the migrants involved. The distinction between internal and international migration is not always precise when territories within a country are more or less autonomous.
 - **803-2**  Simple commuting across a national border receives the name of **border traffic**, and should not be mistaken for international migration.
 - **803-4**  **Immigration**, n. - **immigrate**, v. - **immigrant**, n. and adj.
 - **803-5**  **Emigration**, n. - **emigrate**, v. - **emigrant**, n. and adj.
ctx_en.en:200:
When an individual migrates several times during a certain period, his or her moves may be distinguished according to the **order of migration** **(804-1)**. The **duration of residence** **(804-2)** or **duration of stay** **(804-2)** refers either to the interval between the arrival in a place and the subsequent departure for another destination or to the interval since the most recent move. **Return migration** **(804-3)** involves movement back either to the initial area, or to any previous place of residence. **Repeat migration** **(804-4)** or **chronic migration** **(804-4)** refers to a tendency to migrate several times over a relatively short time interval. **Rural-urban migration** **(804-5)** sometimes takes the form of **serial migration** **(804-6)**, **stage migration** **(804-6)** or **step migration** **(804-6)**, as migrants tend to move to large cities as a final place of destination by a series of shorter, intermediate migrations to cities or areas of successively larger size. The **serial migrations** **(804-7)** between a series of cities of different sizes is sometimes used when net migration of each city is positive and results from an excess of in-migration from the rural sector and smaller cities over emigration to the larger cities.
 - **804-3**  Individuals involved in return migration are called **return migrants**.
 - **804-4**  When repeat migration involves moving to new areas, some authors talk of **secondary migration** and of **secondary migrants**, in contrast to **primary migration** which involves first order or **primary migrants**. This is a source of confusion, since these terms usually take the meaning of 806-4.
ctx_en.en:201:
The contribution of *migration* (801-3) to overall *population growth*  or **population growth due to migration** **(805-1)** (701-1) is due to **net migration** **(805-2)**, i.e., the difference between the number of **arrivals** **(805-3)** and the number of **departures** **(805-4)**. Net migration can have a negative or a positive sign; **net immigration** **(805-5)** or **net in-migration** **(805-5)** is used when arrivals exceed departures, and **net emigration** **(805-6)** or **net out-migration** **(805-6)** when the opposite is true. The sum of arrivals and departures in a country can be used to measure the **volume of migration** **(805-7)**. A similar concept, applied to sub-areas of a country, is the migration **turnover** **(805-8)**. The **net stream** **(805-9)** or **net interchange** **(805-9)** of migration between two areas is defined as the difference between the *stream* (803-9) and the *counterstream* (803-11), whereas the **gross interchange** **(805-10)** is the sum of stream and counterstream.
 - **805-2**  This may also be called the **balance of migration** or the **migration balance**. Terms such as "net migrant" should be avoided, and phrases such as the **net number of migrants** should be preferred.
ctx_en.en:202:
**Spontaneous migration** **(806-1)**, **voluntary migration** **(806-1)** or **free migration** **(806-1)** is the result of the initiative and free choice of the migrants. In the absence of concerted action, the movement is referred to as **individual migration** **(806-2)**. When entire families are moving together, the term **family migration** **(806-3)** is sometimes encountered. **Secondary migration** **(806-4)** or **ancillary migration** **(806-4)** is induced by the movement of others, as when children follow the head of the family. An example of such migration is **family reunification** **(806-9)**, which pertains to the migration of family members, including children, of the family head.  The movement of workers or of members of the labor force in response to employment opportunities is referred to as **labor migration** **(806-5)**. Moves occurring as a result of marriage and when individuals retire from the labor force are sometimes referred to respectively as **marriage migration** **(806-6)** or **retirement migration** **(806-7)**. **Chain migration** **(806-8)** or **linked migration** **(806-8)** refers to a pattern of migration to specific places of destination, where a prospective migrant has a *relative* (114-3*) or friend who has established a residence and is willing to provide information and support.
 - **806-4**  Although the terms are sometimes used in a different sense (cf. 804-4*), a **primary migrant** is the person who makes the actual migration decision while a **secondary migrant** is an individual such as a young child whose migration is the result of another person’s decision.
ctx_en.en:203: Where groups of individuals or families decide to migrate together **collective migration** **(807-1)** or **group migration** **(807-1)** will result. **Mass migration** **(807-2)** involves a very large number of migrants. The term **exodus** **(807-3)** may be used for a sudden mass migration caused by some emergency or catastrophe.
ctx_en.en:204:
*Voluntary migration* (806-1) contrasts with **forced migration** **(808-1)**, in which individuals are compelled by public authorities to move. **Repatriation** **(808-2)** applies to forced return of individuals to their country of origin. Another example of forced migration is the **expulsion** **(808-3)** from their places of abode either of individuals or of whole groups of people. The term **evacuation** **(808-4)** is generally reserved for the movement of whole populations in order to safeguard them from some catastrophe, such as earthquakes, floods, operations of war or the like. A **refugee** **(808-5)** has usually migrated on his own volition, though there may have been strong pressure on him to migrate because his continued stay in his country of origin may have exposed him to danger of persecution. A **displaced person** **(808-6)** is a person who has been moved by a public authority from his place of origin. This move may have taken place as a result of large-scale **displacement of population** **(808-7)** or **population transfer** **(808-7)**, or **population exchange** **(808-8)**.
 - **808-2**  **Repatriation**, n. - **repatriate, v**.
 - **808-3**  **Expulsion**, n. - **expel**, v - **expellee**, n., one who has been expelled. The term **deportation** is used for expulsion of an individual person from his country of residence because his continued residence is considered undesirable by the authorities. **Deportation**, n. - **deport**, v. - **deportee**, n.
 - **808-4**  **Evacuation**, n. **evacuate**, v, - **evacuee**, n., a person who has been evacuated.
ctx_en.en:205: The process by which immigrants adjust themselves to conditions in the area of destination falls into several categories: *naturalization* (331-1), the acquisition of legal citizenship; **absorption** **(809-1)** the entry into productive economic activity; **assimilation** **(809-3)**, integration into the social structure on terms of equality; and **acculturation** **(809-2)** the adoption of the customs and values of the population in the place of destination.
ctx_en.en:206:
When immigrants from a particular territory do not assimilate in their new country but retain the customs of their *place of origin* (801-3), they are called a **colony** **(810-1)**. This raises problems of **coexistence** **(810-2)** between different populations. These may be solved by the **fusion** **(810-3)** of the populations, i.e. by the disappearance of recognizable differences, or by the **integration** **(810-4)** of one of the populations into the other. **Segregation** **(810-5)** exists in a territory where two or more populations live but remain separated by barriers imposed by custom or by the force of law. - **810-1** **Colony**, n. **colonize**, v., to found a colony, also used in the sense of settling a new territory - **colonist**, n., member of a colony. - **810-2** **Coexistence**, n.-**coexist**, v. - **810-5** **Segregation**, n. - **segregate**, v.
In extreme cases, the conflict may result in **genocide**, i.e. an attempt by one population to exterminate the other. **Exterminate**, v. - **extermination**, n.
ctx_en.en:207: **Migration policy** **(811-1)** is one aspect of *population policy* (105-2). Most countries through their **immigration laws** **(811-2)**, restrict the admittance of foreign nationals. These laws frequently provide for **selective immigration** **(811-3)** of persons with certain specified characteristics. Some countries have established **quota systems** **(811-4)** whereby the number of immigrants is fixed in relation to the **national origin** **(811-5)**. Measures designed to influence the **redistribution of population** **(811-6)** within a country through *internal migration* (803-1) are usually more indirect in character.
ctx_en.en:208:
**Migration statistics** **(812-1)** are compiled to reveal the volume of migration, the direction of migratory movement and the characteristics of migrants. The accuracy with which each of these kinds of facts is ascertained depends upon the method of compilation, as most migration statistics consists of approximations and estimates rather than precise measurements. **Direct measurement of migration** **(812-2)** requires a system of recording movements as they occur. The most complete migration statistics are developed from population registers in which all changes of residence are recorded. They allow measurement of internal and of international migration, but are more satisfactory for the former than for the latter. In countries where these population registers do not exist, a certain number of administrative record systems which do not cover the entire population can be used for particular purposes. Thus, **voter registration records** **(812-3)**, **social security records** **(812-4)**  **tax-payers records** **(812-5)** or **dwelling records** **(812-6)** may yield information on internal migration. In the case of overseas migration, statistics may be based on **passenger lists** **(812-7)** or **manifests** **(812-7)** of ships and aircraft. Counts of persons crossing a political frontier yield only very crude data; most of all in areas with much *frontier traffic* (803-2*) special steps must be taken to distinguish migrants from **travellers** **(812-8)**, who do not change their place of residence, and persons in *transit* 801-11). The number of **visas** **(812-9)** or **entry permits** **(812-9)** granted and the number of **residence permits** **(812-10)** or **labor permits** **(812-11)** issued may also be used as an indication of the migration of foreign nationals.
 - **812-8**  **Traveller**, n. - **travel**, v. - **travel**, n.: the process of travelling.
 - **812-9**  In certain countries residents who wish to travel abroad are required to obtain **exit permits** or **exit visas**, records of which may serve as a source of information on migratory movements.
ctx_en.en:209: Information collected in censuses and surveys allows the development of **statistics on migrants** **(813-1)**. Depending on the questions asked, these usually include **statistics on in-migrants** **(813-2)**, **statistics on out-migrants** **(813-2)** and **place-of-birth statistics** **(813-3)**. This approach has limits for the study of international migration; emigrants cannot be studied, whereas immigrants are known, whatever their country of origin.
ctx_en.en:210:
Where it is not possible to determine migration directly, indirect estimates of net migration may be obtained by the **residual method** **(814-1)** or **method of residues** **(814-1)** in which the change in population between two dates is compared with the change due to natural growth; the difference between the two figures is attributed to migration. The **vital statistics method** **(814-2)** consists of computing the difference between total population change, as assessed from two censuses, and *natural increase* (701-7) during the intercensal period. The **survival ratio method** **(814-3)** is commonly used to estimate net migration by age; it does not require actual death statistics. *Survival ratios* are derived from life tables and are applied to a sub-population in one census to give expected numbers by age at the time of the other census. A comparison between the observed and the expected population may be used to estimate the balance of migration by age for the subpopulation. When **place-of-birth statistics** **(814-4)** (813-3) by age and current residence are available in two consecutive censuses, it is possible to make indirect estimates of migration streams.
 - **814-2**  The equation showing that the difference between total population change and natural increase is equal to migration has sometimes received the name of **balancing equation**. In order to use it for the estimation of net migration, one must assume that *omissions* (230-3) and *multiple countings* (230-5) are equal for both censuses.
 - **814-3**  The major variants of this procedure are called the **life table survival ratio method** and the **national census survival ratio method**. In the **forward survival ratio method**, the population at the beginning of an intercensal period serves to estimate the expected population at the end of the period, and the procedure is reversed in the **reverse survival ratio method**; the **average survival ratio method** combines these two approaches.
ctx_en.en:211:
The generic term **migration rate** **(815-1)** refers to any rate which measures the relative frequency of migration within a population. Unless indicated otherwise these rates should be taken as **annual migration rates** **(815-2)**. They may be obtained as the ratio of the average annual number of movements during a certain period, to the average population of the period. An **annual rate of net migration** **(815-3)** and an **annual rate of total migration** **(815-4)** are calculated in a similar fashion by using the appropriate information on net and total migration. An **index of migration effectiveness** **(815-5)** or **effectiveness index** **(815-5)** is calculated as the ratio of net migration to total in- and out-migration. The range of the index is from zero, when arrivals and departures are equal in number, to one, when migration is entirely one way.
 - **815-2**  Other denominators may serve to compute the rate, such as the population at the beginning or the end of the period, or the number of person-years lived by the population of the area.
 - **815-5**  Also: **Index of migration efficiency** or **efficiency index**.
ctx_en.en:212:
**Proportions of migrants** **(816-1)** can be obtained by relating the number of migrants during a period to the population to which or from which they are migrating. When the **proportion of out-migrants** **(816-2)** is obtained by dividing the number who reported moving out of the area by the population residing in the area at the beginning of the period and alive at the end, this index measures the probability of moving for the population at risk, and among other uses, it can be used in the preparation of population projections where migration is accounted for separately. But other populations are often used in practice as denominators to compute proportions of migrants. Similarly, the **proportion of in-migrants** **(816-3)** is sometimes obtained by dividing the number of in-migrants in an area during a period, by the population of the area at the end of the period; but the denominator could also be the population at the beginning of the period, or the average of the beginning and end populations. The **proportion of lifetime in-migrants** **(816-4)** can be derived from information on the place of birth, dividing the number of persons born out of the area by the enumerated population of the area. The **proportion of lifetime out-migrants** **(816-5)** can be obtained by dividing the number of persons in a country living outside of their area of origin, either by the total number of persons born in that area, or by those among them who still live there. When such characteristics of the migrants as *age* (322-1), *occupation* (352-2) or *level of education* (342-1) are known, **indices of migration differentials** **(816-6)** are used to contrast the migrants and the rest of the population of destination. The index is equal to the quantity 1 minus the ratio of the proportion of migrants in the population having the characteristic studied to the proportion of migrants in the whole population. The index of migration differentials is equal to zero when the population with the given characteristic has the same migration behavior as the rest of the population. The term **selectivity of migration** **(816-7)** indicates that the comparison is between the in-migrants and the population from which they were drawn, at the area of origin (801-4). When comparing the characteristics of the in-migrants  to those of the population at the place of arrival (801-5) the term **migration difference** **(816-8)** is sometimes used. 
 - **816-7**  For example, the selectivity of migration from Mexico was decreasing because differences in characteristics between migrants and nonmigrants fade over time; also the origins of Mexican immigrants was increasingly diverse because of the spread of  Mexican **migration networks** in the USA.
ctx_en.en:213: **Longitudinal migration analysis** **(817-1)** requires information on the successive moves of an individual over time, information which is normally available only from *population registers* (213-1) or *retrospective surveys* (203-8). Several refined measures of migration are available from this type of data, such as a **first migration probability** **(817-2)**, defined as the probability that a group of **non-migrants** **(817-3)** aged x will be involved in migration for the first time before reaching age x + n . These probabilities can be used to calculate a **non-migrant table** **(817-4)**. The latter, when combined with a *life table* (432-3) will lead to a double decrement **survivorship schedule of non-migrants** **(817-5)**. Similarly, **migration probabilities by order of move** **(817-6)** can be computed, as well as the proportion of migrants of a given order who have not gone on to make a subsequent move within a certain migration defining interval. The **all orders migration rate** **(817-7)** is the ratio of moves of all orders in a year to the average population size of the *cohort* (116-2) over the year. The cumulation of these rates for a cohort up to a given date provides an estimate of the **mean number of moves** **(817-8)** in the absence of mortality. A survivorship schedule can be combined with an age-specific **all orders migration table** **(817-9)** to estimate the average number of remaining moves for an individual of a given age, given the prevailing mortality.
ctx_en.en:214:
In studying migrants between two areas during a period, one commonly used measure is the **index of migration intensity** **(818-1)**, obtained by dividing the number of migrants from area A to area B by the product of the number of inhabitants in B at the end of the period, and the number of inhabitants of A at the beginning of the period who are still alive at the end. This index, divided by the ratio of the total number of migrants to the square of the population of the country, yields a **migration preference index** **(818-2)**. When the numerator is restricted to the net stream of migration, the resulting measure is called an **index of net velocity** **(818-3)**. The **effectiveness of migration streams** **(818-4)** is measured by relating the absolute value of the net migration stream to the *gross interchange* (805-10).
 - **818-1**  This index can be interpreted as the probability that two individuals alive at the end of the period selected randomly, one among those residing in area A at the beginning of the period, and the other among those residing in B at the end of the period, will be identical. The availability of data may impose various other denominators.
ctx_en.en:215:
**Migration models** **(819-1)** fall in two broad categories. The first relates *migration streams* (803-9) between two areas to social, economic or demographic variables. These variables are often classified as **push factors** **(819-2)** when they characterize **repulsion** **(819-2)** from the area of origin, as **pull factors** **(819-3)** resulting in **attraction** **(819-3)** to the area of destination, and as **intervening obstacles** **(819-4)** between the two areas. The simplest of these models are **gravity models** **(819-5)**: the streams between the two areas are directly proportional to the size of their population, and inversely proportional to the **distance** **(819-6)** between them, raised to a certain power. Other models consider that the streams are proportional to the opportunities in the area of destination, and inversely proportional to **intervening opportunities** **(819-7)** between origin and destination. Models in the second broad category are *stochastic models* (730-5) and refer to individuals rather than to populations; they link the probability of migrating to a certain number of personal characteristics such as age or the previous history of migration.
 - **819-5**  Or **Pareto-type models**.
 - **819-6**  Distance can be measured in diverse ways: a straight line, the route, the number of intervening areas, etc.
ctx_en.en:216: A part of *population theory* (105-1) is concerned with the social and economic determinants and consequences of population trends. The theoretical treatment of population was largely centered in the past on the relation between total population and **resources** **(901-1)**, i.e., the means available to maintain the population, or **production** **(901-2)**, the creation of goods and services. More recently, the emphasis has shifted to the interrelations between *population growth* (701-1) and its components, and *economic growth* (903-1), particularly with respect to **consumption** **(901-3)**, **saving** **(901-4)**, **investment** **(901-5)** and **labor market** **(901-6)**.
ctx_en.en:217:
Consideration of the relations between population size and resources leads to the concepts of **overpopulation** **(902-1)** and **underpopulation** **(902-2)**. These terms are defined only at a given fixed **level of development** **(902-3)**. When neither a larger nor a smaller population would yield advantages, there is said to be an **optimum population** **(902-4)**, sometimes briefly called an **optimum** **(902-4)**. The advantages yielded may be economic in character and in that case it is an **economic optimum** **(902-5)**. The discussion of economic optima generally proceeds in terms of economic welfare but, as this is difficult to ascertain empirically, the **level of living** **(902-6)** or **standard of living** **(902-6)** is sometimes substituted. This is approximated by the **real national income per capita** **(902-7)** i.e., the total amount of goods and services produced in a particular period (or its equivalent in money income adjusted for variation in purchasing power) divided by the total population during the period.
 - **902-1**  **Overpopulation**, n. - **overpopulated**, adj.
 - **902-2**  **Underpopulation**, n. - **underpopulated**, adj.
 - **902-5**  Some writers have used the concept of a **power optimum** and a **social optimum** as well as of an **economic optimum**.
 - **902-6**  The expression "standard of living" is restricted by some economists to mean an accepted goal or recognized set of needs, as constrasted with the level of living actually attained. Others use these terms interchangeably. 
 - **902-7**  Other measures such as the **gross national product per capita**, are also used.
ctx_en.en:218:
Economists have emphasized the dynamic relations between **economic growth** **(903-1)** or **economic development** **(903-1)** and rates of population growth and changes in population structure; they are less interested today in the static concept of an optimum size, than in the dynamic concept of the **optimum rate of growth** **(903-2)** of population, i.e., the rate of growth which will be consistent with the maximum rate of increase of the level of living. These relations are of particular concern in countries with a low level of living, which have come to be called **less developed countries** **(903-3)** or **developing countries** **(903-3)**.
 - **903-3**  Also: **underdeveloped countries** or **low-income countries**. They are commonly contrasted with the **developed countries**, or **more developed countries**.
ctx_en.en:219: The **maximum population** **(904-1)** of a territory, sometimes called its **carrying capacity** **(904-1)**, is generally understood in an absolute sense to mean the largest number of persons that could be sustained under specified conditions; but is sometimes used to denote the largest number that could be supported at an assumed standard of living. Conversely, the **minimum population** **(904-2)** is generally taken to be the smallest number of persons in an area which is consistent with **group survival** **(904-3)**.
ctx_en.en:220:
The term **population pressure** **(905-1)** is linked to concepts relating the size of the population and the *resources* (901-1) available. To say that this pressure is strong or weak in a certain area is to suggest that the population of the area is near or far from the maximum consistent with the resources which are available. According to **Malthusian population theory** **(905-2)**, so called after its originator, Thomas Malthus, there will inevitably be pressure of population on the **means of subsistence** **(905-3)**. Any change in the volume of available means of subsistence would generate *population growth* (701-1) until **population equilibrium** **(905-4)** would again be attained when the level of living had reached a **subsistence level** **(905-5)**, i.e., a level just sufficient to maintain life. The equilibrium would be maintained by the elimination of any **surplus population** **(905-10)** either through **positive checks** **(905-6)**, sometimes known as **Malthusian checks** **(905-6)** (famine, pestilence and war), or through the **preventive check** **(905-7)** of **moral restraint** **(905-8)** consisting of **postponement of marriage** **(905-9)**, coupled with abstinence from sexual relations before marriage.
 - **905-6**  and 7. The terms **positive check** and **preventive check** in English are generally used only with reference to the doctrines of Malthus.
ctx_en.en:221:
Although the term **Malthusianism** **(906-1)** originally refers to the theories of Malthus, it is often used today to denote the doctrine that a check in the rate of population growth is desirable. **Neo-Malthusianism** **(906-2)**, whilst accepting the desirability of checking population growth, advocates that such restriction should be achieved through the use of *birth control methods* (627-3).
 - **906-1**  **Malthusianism**, n. - **Malthusian**, adj.: conforming to the doctrines of Malthus. The terms are sometimes used mistakenly to refer to the advocacy of family planning programs to solve economic problems.
ctx_en.en:222:
The process of transition from a situation in which both fertility and mortality were relatively high to one in which they are relatively low which has been observed in many countries, is called the **demographic transition** **(907-1)** or **population transition** **(907-1)**. In the process of moving from a **pre-transitional stage** **(907-2)** to a **post-transitional stage** **(907-3)**, there is typically a lag between the declines of mortality and fertility, so that a stage of **transitional growth** **(907-4)** of population results. Economists have studied changes in **productivity** **(907-5)**, i.e., production per member of the labor force, or per head of the population, associated with this transitional period.
 - **907-1**  Sometimes called the **vital revolution**. A further distinction is made between the **fertility transition** and the **mortality transition**. The **theory of the demographic transition** associates historical changes in vital rates with socio-economic transformations attending the process of industrialization and urbanization.
ctx_en.en:223:
In **eugenics** **(910-1)**, a theory which examined the role of  **heredity** **(910-2)**, the transmission of **hereditary characteristics** **(910-3)**, such as the color of the eyes, from generation to generation. **Acquired characteristics** **(910-4)** are not so transmitted. A **lethal characteristic** **(910-5)** generally brings about the early death of the foetus.
 - **910-1**  **Eugenics**, n. - **eugenic**, adj. - **eugenist**, n.: a specialist in eugenics.
 - **910-2**  **Heredity**, n. - **hereditary**, adj.
ctx_en.en:224:
The transmission of hereditary characteristics operates through **genes** **(911-1)** which are transmitted to children by their parents. **Genetics** **(911-2)** is the science concerned with the transmission and effects of hereditary factors. The genes are carried by **chromosomes** **(911-3)** which are long filaments of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) located in the cell’s nucleus. The position of a gene on a chromosome is called its **locus** **(911-4)**. Genes occupying the same locus affect the same characteristic, although they do so in various ways which correspond to various **alleles** **(911-5)** of the gene in this locus. The new cell formed by the union of two sexual cells or **gametes** **(911-6)** during the process of *conception* (602-1) is called a **zygote** **(911-7)**.
 - **911-1**  All of the genes carried by an individual are collectively called his or her **genetic endowment**.
 - **911-2**  **Genetics**, n. - **genetic**, adj. - **geneticist**, n.: a specialist in genetics.
ctx_en.en:225:
The set of two genes of an individual at the same locus is called a **genotype** **(912-1)**; the genotype is said to be **homozygous** **(912-2)** if the alleles are identical at a given locus; it is said to be **heterozygous** **(912-3)** in the opposite case. The **phenotype** **(912-4)** consists in the observable characteristics as determined by the genotype and the environment. If an heterozygous individual (AA’) cannot be distinguished from an homozygous individual (AA), the allele A is said to be **dominant** **(912-5)** over allele A’, and A’ is said to be **recessive** **(912-6)**. Genes are subject to sudden and apparently random changes, called **mutations** **(912-7)**. **Panmixia** **(912-8)** or **random mating** **(912-8)** insures uniform distribution of genes within populations.
 - **912-7**  **Mutation**, n. - **mutant**, adj. or n.
